never as a mismatch: a read that failed is no evidence about the review. Two differences from
creation remain. An ambiguous access package NAME on this path is published as the resolver's own
`AmbiguousName` record, while `New-OERAccessReviewDefinition` maps the same ambiguity to
`AmbiguousAccessPackageName`; both are `Ambiguous*` ids. And a declared access package GUID is not
read on this path, so a stale one is refused as `AccessReviewScopeMismatch`, where creation's
existence read publishes `AccessPackageNotFound`. A policy GUID is not read on either path. If wrong:
rename the id before the stable release; nothing depends on it but the record.

**Rule 3 (the handler).** The check is the first statement for an existing review in
`Sync-OERStructureAccessReview`, before the reviewer lookups, the diff and `ShouldProcess`. On a
record the handler writes it through `$Caller.WriteError`, reports one `Failed` row carrying it, and
returns, so a plan and a real run report the same row and nothing further is read or written for the
entry. The row's Detail is the record's message for the refusal. For any other record it reads as
below; a not-found message ends with a period, so there it reads `... not found.; nothing was written`.

`could not resolve the access package or assignment policy of access review '<name>': <message>; nothing was written`

The `NotApplied` scope note in the pure diff is kept unchanged: the handler never reaches it with
another scope now, since a GUID that differs is refused before the diff and a name is not compared by
the diff, and its help says so. If wrong: the note is dead weight in the handler path only.

**Rule 4 (the policy lookup, extracted; `Resolve-OERAssignmentPolicyId`).** The assignment policy name
lookup moved, unchanged, out of `Resolve-OERAccessReviewScopeTarget` into its own helper, so the
update path resolves a policy name exactly as creation does: a GUID is returned as written; a name
lists the package's policies once and returns the one id, `$null` for no match, and throws an
`AmbiguousName` record, with the message as before, for several; a listing that fails propagates.
`Resolve-OERAccessReviewScopeTarget` keeps its result shapes, and its own test file passed unchanged,
which is the refactor's proof. If wrong: duplicating the lookup was the alternative, and the review
rubric refuses it.

**Rule 5 (the guard lists).** `tests/Unit/Public/AmbiguousName.Guard.Tests.ps1` lists the PUBLIC
cmdlets that call a `Resolve-OER*Id` helper directly; the engine reaches the helpers through a private
handler, so its ambiguity and 403 cases are proven in the handler's tests and the helper's tests
instead. `Get-OERAccessReviewTargetMismatch` reads `accessPackage` and `assignmentPolicy` through
`Test-OERDeclaredProperty`, so it joined gate 8's named list of document consumers
([#static-source-gates](#static-source-gates)). If wrong: one guard case to add.

Nothing here was measured live: the rules were derived from the code and proven with mocked tests.

**Since Sprint 11 step 4b.** The check also runs on a review found under the `previousDisplayName` its
entry declares, before the review is renamed or anything else is written to it, and its `Failed` row
then says where the review was found. An `accessPackage` or `assignmentPolicy` name for which the
run's rename map holds an id, a package or policy the same document renames, is compared as that id,
as written, with no lookup (`## rename-policies-and-reviews`, D5 and D6). Since Sprint 11 step 6 the
map holds the id of every access package the document declares, renamed or not, so an `accessPackage`
name the document declares is compared as the id of the package its entry found or created, and never
looked up in the whole tenant ([#review-package-in-the-same-run](#review-package-in-the-same-run)).

**Since Sprint 11 step 5.** The export no longer writes a shared name here: `Get-OERInventory` sends
the same two lookups this check sends and keeps a review's `accessPackage` or `assignmentPolicy` name
only when the lookup finds that object and no other, and writes the id otherwise, so an export
re-applied unchanged is no longer refused for a shared name. The rule above is unchanged: a document
that names a shared package or policy is still refused with `AmbiguousName`. The export's lookups are
a named deviation from the single owner of the policy lookup, held in step by an agreement test
([#roster-identity-and-shared-names](#roster-identity-and-shared-names)).

## policy-update-keeps-custom-extensions

Sprint 11 step 3 made `Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy` stop dropping what Microsoft Graph
removes from an assignment policy on a full PUT. The cmdlet is a read-modify-write: it reads the live
policy once, and `ConvertTo-OERPolicyBody` carries whatever the command line did not name into the
body of the PUT. Until this step that was the scope, the requestor and approval settings, the
expiration, `reviewSettings` and `questions`, and nothing else the read held. So a description-only
update of a policy with a custom extension stage removed the stage, and the update of the measured
automatic assignment policy (one `attributeRuleMembers` target) was refused (M3).
`Invoke-OERStructure` reaches a policy through the same cmdlet, so it
follows the rules below too. The facts marked M1 to M5 were measured live on 2026-10-13 as the test
identity `oer-live-cc` in the operator's test tenant, and no tenant value is recorded here. The rest
was derived from the code and proven with mocked tests.

**M1 (what the read returns).** `GET .../assignmentPolicies/{id}` with no query, with
`$expand=accessPackage` (the module's read) and with `$expand=customExtensionStageSettings` returns
`automaticRequestSettings` (null on a request-based policy, the object on an automatic one),
`questions` (in full) and `customExtensionStageSettings`, the last as `[{ id, stage }]` only: the
custom extension's own id is read only with
`$expand=customExtensionStageSettings($expand=customExtension)`.
`$expand=accessPackage,customExtensionStageSettings($expand=customExtension)` answers 200 with both.
`$expand=questions` is refused (400 InvalidFilter, "not a navigation property or complex property").
The policy carries `notificationSettings`; there is no `accessPackageNotificationSettings`.

**M2 (a description-only update loses the stages).** A description-only
`Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy` (the code of this branch's base, d9a13cc) on a request-based
policy with one custom extension stage (`assignmentRequestCreated`) and one text question sent a PUT
body that carried `accessPackage, allowedTargetScope, description, displayName, expiration, id,
notificationSettings, questions, requestApprovalSettings, requestorSettings, specificAllowedTargets`.
Afterwards `customExtensionStageSettings` read `[]` -- REMOVED by Microsoft Graph -- and every other
field, the question included, was unchanged.

**M3 (an automatic policy's update is refused without its settings).** The same update on an automatic
assignment policy (`allowedTargetScope` specificDirectoryUsers, one `attributeRuleMembers` target,
`automaticRequestSettings` set) was refused: 400 `InvalidSpecificAllowedTargets`, "If the allowed
target scope is set to specific targets, at least one valid target must be provided." Nothing changed.

**M4 (with the settings it is accepted).** The body `ConvertTo-OERPolicyBody` builds for that update,
plus the live `automaticRequestSettings`, sent raw: 200. `automaticRequestSettings`,
`specificAllowedTargets` and `allowedTargetScope` were unchanged and the description changed.

**M5 (the stages go back in the documented shape).** A raw PUT of the request-based policy carrying
`customExtensionStageSettings` with one entry, `stage` `assignmentRequestCreated` and a
`customExtension` holding `@odata.type` `#microsoft.graph.accessPackageAssignmentRequestWorkflowExtension`
and the extension's id (the documented shape, Microsoft Learn "Update accessPackageAssignmentPolicy",
example 3) answered 200, and the stage was back on the next read.

**Rule 1 (the stages are carried; `ConvertTo-OERPolicyBody`).** The live `customExtensionStageSettings`
is carried into the PUT whenever it holds at least one stage, in the shape of M5: per stage the
`stage` and a `customExtension` holding the extension's `@odata.type` (when the read returned one) and
its `id`, and nothing else -- no stage id, no display name, no endpoint configuration. A stage with no
`customExtension`, or one with no `id`, makes the helper throw instead: dropping it would disconnect
the extension, which is the loss this rule exists to prevent, so the helper fails closed.
`Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy` publishes that as a non-terminating `InvalidPolicyInput`, before
its `ShouldProcess` gate and so also under `-WhatIf`, and sends no update; the message ends with the
way forward (read the policy with its custom extension stages, or remove the stage). An empty or absent list adds
no key, so a policy without stages is PUT exactly as before. If wrong: a policy whose extension id the
read cannot return (a permission, say) cannot be updated by this cmdlet until that is fixed, which is
a refusal with nothing sent where the old code sent a silent loss. The shape was measured only for one
stage name and one extension type (M5); other stages and the other extension type are carried in the
same documented shape, which is not measured.

**Rule 2 (the automatic settings travel with the scope).** The live `automaticRequestSettings` is
carried into the PUT only when it is non-null AND `-RequestorScope` was not passed. It goes as one unit
with the carried `allowedTargetScope` and `specificAllowedTargets` (M3, M4), so an automatic policy is
updated without losing its rule. A declared scope never inherits automatic assignment: the declared
scope replaces the allowed targets, and carrying the settings over would let the package be assigned
automatically to whoever the new scope names. A request-based policy has the value null and gets no
key. If wrong: an operator who passes `-RequestorScope` for an automatic policy sends a body without
the settings, and Microsoft Graph decides; M3 shows it refuses an automatic policy's update without
them when the target is a specific one, and the outcome with a declared scope was not measured. A
refused update changes nothing (M3).

**Rule 3 (the read expands the extension; one GET).** `Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy` still
reads the policy once, for the access package id and as the baseline of the update, and the request is
now `v1.0/identityGovernance/entitlementManagement/assignmentPolicies/{id}` with
`$expand=accessPackage,customExtensionStageSettings($expand=customExtension)`, the combined expansion
M1 measured as 200. `$expand=accessPackage` alone returns a stage as `{ id, stage }` without the
extension's own id, and the id is what Rule 1 sends back. `$expand=questions` is refused, so `questions`
is read without it (it comes in full). If wrong: a Graph version that refused the combined expansion
would fail the read for every policy, visibly and with nothing sent; restoring the narrower expansion
would bring the loss back unless the id is read another way.

**What the document cannot say.** `Invoke-OERStructure` has no key for a custom extension stage or for
automatic assignment, so neither is ever declared: they are only preserved, like `reviewSettings` and
`questions`. The automatic assignment settings are preserved only while the entry declares no
`requestorScope` (Rule 2); an entry that declares one is sent without them.

## rename-refused-outside-groups

Sprint 11 step 3 (BL-128, decision A5) made `Test-OERStructureSchema` refuse a `previousDisplayName`
where the engine cannot rename, and made a `-WhatIf` plan report a package in a new catalog as
created. This anchor records the problem, the rules, and what each costs if it is wrong. Nothing here
was measured live; the rules were derived from the code and proven with mocked tests. Sprint 11 step 4
later made administrative units, catalogs and access packages renameable (`## rename-more-object-kinds`),
and step 4b assignment policies and access reviews (`## rename-policies-and-reviews`), so the refusal
of Rule 1 below is gone: the validator refuses `previousDisplayName` on no kind, and Rule 1 is the record
of what steps 3 and 4 did. Rule 3 is unaffected. Rule 2 holds except that an access package declaring
`previousDisplayName` in a catalog the plan would create is not planned as created: nothing can be
renamed in a catalog that does not exist yet, so it fails with `AccessPackageRenameNotFound`; and an
assignment policy declaring it in a package the plan would create fails with
`AssignmentPolicyRenameNotFound` instead of its `would create assignmentPolicy` row.

**The problem (BL-128).** Until step 4 only the groups handler read `previousDisplayName`. The other
sections -- `administrativeUnits`, `catalogs`, `accessPackages` and an access package's
`assignmentPolicies`, and `accessReviews` -- match an entry by its `displayName` (a package within
its catalog, a policy within its package) and create what they do not find. A document that declared
`previousDisplayName` there, copied from a group rename say, was accepted without a word: the key was
ignored, nothing was found under the new name, and the engine created a second object beside the one
the operator meant to rename. The old object stayed in place, unreported.

**Rule 1 (the refusal; `Test-OERStructureSchema`).** Step 3 made a `previousDisplayName` present and
not null on an administrative unit, a catalog, an access package, an assignment policy of an access
package or an access review an `Error` at `previousDisplayName` under that entry's path, so the whole
document is refused before authentication and before any write. Step 4 took the first three out of
the refusal when the engine began to rename them, so the `Error` now stands for an assignment policy
and an access review. The message states that only groups, administrative units, catalogs and access
packages can be renamed through the document, that the engine does not read `previousDisplayName` for
that kind and so would create a new object named by `displayName` beside the existing one, and the way
out (remove the key, rename the existing object outside the document first); it names the kind with
the article its first letter calls for. An earlier wording said the engine "matches by displayName
alone", which was inexact (a package is matched within its catalog, a policy within its package) and
is gone; and the step 3 wording said that only groups can be renamed, which step 4 made false. A group,
a unit, a catalog and a package keep their `previousDisplayName`, which is the rename the engine
supports. An explicit null is not declared, as for every other key (`Test-HasProp` is present and not
null), and is not reported. If wrong: a document that carries the key on an assignment policy or an
access review used to apply and now fails validation; the fix is to remove the key and, when the
object is to be renamed, rename it outside the document first. Step 4b removed the refusal for those
two kinds as well, deleting the validator's `Add-UnsupportedRenameFinding` with both of its call
sites, since the engine now renames them (`## rename-policies-and-reviews`).

**Rule 2 (a package in a catalog the same plan creates; R4).** Under `-WhatIf` a catalog the document
creates does not exist yet, so the catalog-scoped lookup of a package declared in it failed with
`CatalogNotFound` and the plan reported the package `Failed`, "the access package was NOT created",
while the real run creates the catalog and then the package. `Invoke-OERStructure` now makes one list
of catalog names per document and hands it, as `-PlannedCatalog`, to the catalogs handler and the
access package handler only. `Sync-OERStructureCatalog` adds a name to it only when `$WhatIfPreference`
is true and it reports `would create catalog`. `Sync-OERStructureAccessPackage` compares the package's
catalog with the list without regard to letter case and, when it is there, skips the catalog-scoped
lookup and takes the create branch, which under `-WhatIf` reports the plan and returns. A real run
never fills the list, so it is unchanged. A declined `-Confirm` leaves `ShouldProcess` false with
`$WhatIfPreference` false, so it adds nothing and the package stays `Failed`, as a real run would find
it. A package whose catalog the document does not declare and the tenant does not hold is still
`Failed`, and so is one in a declared catalog when `-Include` leaves the catalogs section out, since
the list is then empty. If wrong: a plan can promise a package that the real run reports `Failed`
because its catalog could not be created (a refused write, say); a plan reports what a run would do if
the rows before it succeed, and it cannot know otherwise.

**Rule 3 (the policy rows say create; R5).** In that create branch the policy rows read
`would create assignmentPolicy`, the policy's name in quotes and `after access package is created`; they
read `would configure assignmentPolicy` before. The policy is created, not configured, and the rows now
appear in the plan of a package in a new catalog. The resource role rows keep their `would configure
resourceRole` text. If wrong: a script that matched the old row text no longer matches. The historical
live-verification checklists under `docs/live-verification/` quote the old text as a record of what a
past run printed, and are not edited.

## mail-nickname

Sprint 11 step 3 (BL-132, decision A9) validated `mailNickname`, made `New-OERGroup` refuse an alias it
cannot derive, and made the validator warn when a renamed group keeps an alias that does not follow
the rename. This anchor records the problem, the measurement, the rules and what each costs if it is
wrong.

**The problem (BL-132).** `New-OERGroup` derived the alias from the display name inline, removing every
character outside A-Z, a-z, 0-9, `.`, `_` and `-`, and sent it. A name with none of those characters
derives the empty string, and a long one derives more than 64 characters: Microsoft Graph refuses such
an alias (M6), and the create, after the administrative unit was resolved, was the first place the
module learned of it. The validator accepted
any string for a declared `mailNickname`, so a bad alias failed only at apply. And a group keeps its
alias when it is renamed, so a document that renames a group and leaves `mailNickname` alone leaves the
old name in the group's mail alias, which is rarely what the operator wants.

**M6 (what Microsoft Graph accepts; measured 2026-10-13, as `oer-live-cc`).** `mailNickname`, PATCH on a
security group, app-only: refused (400 Request_BadRequest, "Invalid value specified for property
'mailNickname' of resource 'Group'") for each of `@ ( ) \ [ ] " ; : < > ,`, a space, a tab, the empty
string and 65 characters; accepted (204) for `. - _ / ' ~ ! # $ % & * + = ? ^ { | }`, the backtick, the
non-ASCII letter U+00E5 and 64 characters. The refusal was measured on an update; the create is
expected to apply the same rule and was not measured separately. Two Microsoft Learn pages describe
the property and differ from each other and from the measurement. The "group resource type" page
(`mailNickname`) lists exactly the refused printable set (`@ () \ [] " ; : <> , SPACE`) and says
"maximum length is 64 characters"; it also says ASCII only, which the measurement contradicts (U+00E5
was accepted). The "Update group" page also excludes `.`, which the measurement contradicts too (`.`
was accepted). The rules below follow the measurement, and the printable set is the one the first
page and the measurement agree on.

**Rule 1 (one owner of the derivation; R6).** `Get-OERDerivedMailNickname` is the single owner of the
alias derived from a display name: `-replace '[^A-Za-z0-9._-]', ''`. `New-OERGroup` and the validator
both call it, so the alias the validator compares a rename against is the alias `New-OERGroup` would
have created. It is pure and returns the empty string or a long one as it is; the callers decide what
that means. If wrong: a second copy of the derivation drifts from the first, and the validator would
warn about, or miss, an alias `New-OERGroup` never creates.

**Rule 2 (the refusal in `New-OERGroup`; R7).** When `-MailNickname` is not given and the derived alias
is empty or longer than 64 characters, the command writes the non-terminating `DerivedMailNicknameInvalid`
(category `InvalidArgument`, target the resolved display name) and returns, with nothing sent, also
under `-WhatIf`. The message names the length, or says the alias is empty, says that Microsoft Graph
accepts 1 to 64 characters, and asks for `-MailNickname`. The refusal stands AFTER the idempotent
existence lookup, so a group that already exists is still returned whatever its name derives to (an
existing group needs no alias and a re-run of an apply must stay idempotent), and BEFORE the
administrative unit lookup and the create. An explicit `-MailNickname` is sent as given: the command
does not validate it, and Microsoft Graph refuses a bad one at the create; the document validator is
what catches it for a document (Rule 3). If wrong: moved before the lookup, the check would refuse an
existing group; moved after the unit lookup, it would spend requests on a call that cannot succeed.
A document group that declares no `mailNickname` and whose name derives to an invalid alias is not
caught offline: `Test-OERStructure` and the `-WhatIf` plan accept it, since the plan reports
`would create group` without calling `New-OERGroup`, and the real run reports the entry `Failed` with
`DerivedMailNicknameInvalid`. That is a known limit, not a decision.

**Rule 3 (the validator refuses what Graph was measured to refuse, and a little more; R8).** A declared `mailNickname` that is a string is
an `Error` at its path when it is empty, when it is longer than 64 characters (the message names the
length), and when it contains any of `@ ( ) \ [ ] " ; : < > ,`, white space (`[char]::IsWhiteSpace`) or
a control character (`[char]::IsControl`); the message names each such character once, white space and
control characters by code point. Each rule is its own `Error`, so a value that breaks two reports two.
A non-string value keeps the existing "must be a string" `Error`. A non-ASCII letter and `.` are
accepted, as Microsoft Graph accepted them (M6). White space other than the space and the tab, and
control characters other than the tab, were not measured one by one: they follow the measured refusals
and are refused on the ground that no alias needs them, so the user-facing texts (the `Error`'s own
message, the schema description, the README, the about topic) say that Microsoft Graph was measured to refuse the printable
set, the space, the tab, the empty string and more than 64 characters, and that the validator refuses
the rest too. The schema declares `minLength` 1 and `maxLength` 64 and describes the characters, and
the character set is enforced by the offline validator alone. If wrong: a document whose alias holds such a character that Graph would accept is
refused by the validator; remove the character.

**Rule 4 (the alias does not follow a rename; A5).** A `groups[]` entry with a `previousDisplayName`
that is a non-empty string and differs from `displayName` without regard to letter case is renamed. It
gets a `Warning` at its `mailNickname` path when it declares no `mailNickname` (it keeps its current
alias) or declares one equal, without regard to letter case, to the alias `Get-OERDerivedMailNickname`
derives from the old name. It is a `Warning`, not an `Error`, since keeping the alias can be deliberate
and the document is valid either way. The message says the alias does not follow a rename and what to
declare. A `previousDisplayName` that is an object id, and a template-based group with no
`mailNickname`, warn too although there is no old name to derive an alias from; the message hedges
("if that alias was derived from the old name"). If wrong: one Warning too many on such a document.

### CLAUDE.md text for mail-nickname

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Get-OERDerivedMailNickname` is the single owner of the mail alias `New-OERGroup` derives from a
  display name** (every character outside A-Z, a-z, 0-9, '.', '_' and '-' removed). `New-OERGroup`
  refuses a derived alias that is empty or longer than 64 characters with `DerivedMailNicknameInvalid`,
  and `Test-OERStructureSchema` compares a renamed group's `mailNickname` with the alias derived from
  its previous name. Never re-implement the derivation inline.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#mail-nickname`

## rename-policies-and-reviews

Sprint 11 step 4b (BL-128 part 2, decision A5) made an assignment policy of an access package and an
access review renameable through the apply document, with the rules of `## rename-more-object-kinds`:
`previousDisplayName` names the object's current display name or object id beside the new
`displayName`, both names are resolved on every run before anything else is read or written for the
object, the object found only under the previous name is renamed in the same update as every other
changed property, and an entry whose two names find different objects, or neither finds one, fails
with nothing written. The step also made an access review that names an access package or an
assignment policy renamed in the same run reach it through the run's rename map, made
`Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy` rename a policy given `-DisplayName` alone (A16), and stopped
the catalogs handler from taking a failed read for an empty fact (BL-144). This anchor records the
rules (D1 to D7), the rulings made while planning (P3 to P6) and on the review of the first version
(the marks under a package id in D4, and Rule 15) with what each costs if it is wrong, and the known
limits. Unchanged by this step: `-Prune` never removes an assignment policy or an access
review, the export never writes `previousDisplayName`, `NothingToUpdate` stays the published id for
"nothing to update", and no public parameter or output type was added; the four ids in D1 are the
only new ones. The rules were derived from the code and proven with mocked tests; nothing here has
been measured live yet.

**D1 (the decision owner and the keys).** `Resolve-OERStructureRename` decides for the
`assignmentPolicies` and `accessReviews` sections too, with the outcomes it decides for the other
kinds (`Rename`, `Current`, `Conflict`, `NotFound`, and `Undecided` for a mark) and four new ids:
`AssignmentPolicyRenameConflict` and `AccessReviewRenameConflict` (category `ResourceExists`),
`AssignmentPolicyRenameNotFound` and `AccessReviewRenameNotFound` (category `ObjectNotFound`), each
with the new name as its target. A policy is matched within its access package, so `-AccessPackage`
is required for that section (a caller error, thrown as an `ArgumentException`) and the messages name
the package. The map key of a policy is `assignmentPolicies|<package>|<policy>` in lower case, the
package term being the package's display name as its accessPackages entry declares it; when the
package's id is known at decision time, the same outcome is registered under the key built with the
id as well (the same entry, and a `Current` removes both), so a review that names the package by
object id finds it. An undecided mark is registered the same way: under the name key, and under the
id key for a package id given with it (D4).
`Get-OERStructureRenameTarget` reads the policy keys with `-AccessPackage` (the package's name or
id) and does not serve `accessReviews`. If wrong: a second owner of the policy decision would word
the refusals its own way, and a key built in a third place would drift from the two that build it.

**D2 (a policy's rows are its package's rows).** Every row about a policy, the decision's refusals
included, is a row of its package's entry: section `accessPackages`, the package's display name as
the item, and the policy named in the detail (the decision's rows start with
`assignmentPolicy '<new name>':`), as every policy row of `Sync-OERStructureAccessPackage` already
was. The error record's target is the policy's new name. If wrong: a reader that filters rows by
section finds a policy's rename under its package, where every other policy row has always been.

**The policy handler.** `Sync-OERStructureAccessPackage` matches `previousDisplayName` in the
package's policy list, which it has already read, so it costs no request: an object id matches only
the id of a policy of this package, without regard to letter case (R5 of step 4), and a name matches
a display name without regard to letter case, as `displayName` does. The refusal of a `displayName`
that several live policies carry stays first and unchanged; a previous name that several carry is
refused next, with one `AmbiguousName` record whose target is the previous name and one `Failed`
row, saying to declare the previous name as the policy's object id. A `Rename` acts on the policy
found under the previous name, and the new name travels as `-DisplayName` in its one
`Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy` call with every declared field, which is sent even when no
declared field differs (D3 makes such a call an update). A policy that a declared
`previousDisplayName` names is not reported `Extra`, unless the entry's own `displayName` was refused
first. A policy that declares `previousDisplayName` in a package the call creates, or under `-WhatIf`
would create, fails with `AssignmentPolicyRenameNotFound` and is never created. When the previous
name is an object id, the rename texts name the policy by its current name followed by the id. A
rename sends every declared field, so a renaming policy whose entry declares `requestorScope`
`SpecificConnectedOrganizationUsers` is refused by the existing guard against that scope even when
the scope does not differ; omitting `requestorScope`, the way out the refusal names, renames it. If
wrong: a rename alone would be reported `Unchanged` and never sent, or would reach a policy of
another package.

**D3 (A16; `Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy -DisplayName` alone).** Issue #47 made the cmdlet
refuse, with `NothingToUpdate` and before any request, a call that supplies no updatable property
beyond the mandatory `-DisplayName`. That refused the one call the handler needs for a rename alone.
The cmdlet now decides on the live policy, directly after the GET it already makes: with no other
updatable property bound, a `-DisplayName` equal to the live display name, compared ignoring case, is
`NothingToUpdate` (the same id, category and target, and a message that says how to rename or update
instead), and a different one is a rename, sent as the usual full PUT with everything else carried
forward (`## policy-update-keeps-custom-extensions`). A failed GET is reported as itself, never as
`NothingToUpdate`, and the decision comes before the `AccessPackageNotFound` check, so a read that
carries the live name and no access package is `NothingToUpdate`. A change of letter case alone is
therefore not sent; with another property it is. Cost: a call that issue #47 refused without a
request now costs one GET before `NothingToUpdate`. The decision's `$null -ne $Existing` term is an
equivalent mutant: `-DisplayName` is mandatory and cannot be empty, while a missing read's display
name converts to the empty string, which never equals it; the term stays because it says what the
decision reads. If wrong: the handler would have to re-send a value to make a rename alone an update
(P3's alternative).

**P3 (the NothingToUpdate cohort).** `tests/Unit/Public/NothingToUpdate.Cohort.Tests.ps1` holds every
`Set-OER*` cmdlet to reporting `NothingToUpdate` for a call with no updatable property, and to issuing
no request for it. D3 needs the live name, so for this one cmdlet the case keeps its `Invoke` block and
its expected `NothingToUpdate`, carries a `LivePolicy` (a policy whose display name is the
`-DisplayName` the case passes) that answers its read, and asserts exactly one GET and no write; the
other eleven keep the no-request assertion. If wrong: the architect meant zero requests, which A16
cannot meet; the alternative is the handler re-sending a value, a change confined to the access
package handler.

**D4 (R12 for packages and policies).** `Sync-OERStructureAccessPackage`, as its first action and
before the catalog check and any lookup, marks the package undecided when its entry declares
`previousDisplayName`, and every assignment policy that declares one, with the reason "the
accessPackages entry did not reach a decision in this run; see that entry's rows". Each decision
replaces its mark: the package's under `accessPackages|<name>`, a policy's under both of its keys
(D1). Every early return leaves the marks no decision has replaced yet -- the catalog refused, a
failed or ambiguous lookup, a failed package update that renames it, an ambiguous policy name -- so
a review that names a new name is refused instead of being looked up by name, which could reach
another object that carries that name. The first marks know no package id, so they are under the
name key alone. Every renaming policy is therefore marked again, under the key with a package's id
as well, as soon as the entry knows the id of a package it may mean: the existing package found,
before anything else is read or written for it; both packages of a refused rename conflict; and every
package of the catalog that carries the entry's `displayName`, or its previous name together with the
one that carries the `displayName`, when that name is refused as ambiguous. Those are the controller's
two rulings on the review of the first version, which marked by name alone: without the id key, a
review that names the package by object id looked a policy left undecided up by name within that
package, where another policy may already carry the new name. Cost: one helper in the handler and
four places that call it. A name that is empty after string conversion is not marked: the validator
refuses such an entry, and the helper's parameter binding would otherwise end the item in the mark
block. `Invoke-OERStructure` marks the packages and the policies of a document whose `-Include`
leaves AccessPackages out, with the reason "the accessPackages section is not selected by -Include,
so its rename is not reconciled in this run", each policy that declares `previousDisplayName` whether
or not its package is renamed, under the name keys alone, since nothing is read for the entry. If
wrong: a review that names the new name of a package or policy whose entry stopped would be looked up
by name and could reach another object that carries it. The cost, accepted, is step 4's: while
`-Include` leaves the section out and the entry still declares `previousDisplayName`, every review
that names the new name by name is refused, even when the rename was done in an earlier run (a review
that names the package by object id looks a policy up by name, P6). Since Sprint 11 step 6 (BL-147)
every accessPackages entry is marked, not only one that renames: the package handler marks an entry
that renames nothing as refused until it registers the package's id, and `Invoke-OERStructure` marks
it so when `-Include` leaves the section out, so every review that names a declared package by name is
refused there ([#review-package-in-the-same-run](#review-package-in-the-same-run)).

**D5 (a review reads the map).** `Sync-OERStructureAccessReview` takes `-RenameMap` and reads it,
before any Graph call for the entry, for its `accessPackage` (by name; a GUID is an object id and not a
key) and its `assignmentPolicy` (by name within the package as the review names it, by the package's
name or its object id). An entry that is refused -- a rename that conflicted or found nothing, or a
mark -- gives one `Failed` row naming the refused rename and its reason, no error record of its own
(the rename's own row carries one when it was refused, as step 4's R9 rules), and nothing is
created, read or written for the review, under `-WhatIf` too; the package is read first, so a refused
package stops the review before its policy is read. An entry with an id replaces the name in a copy
of the review entry that only the target check and the create read, so the check compares that id as
written and a new review is created on it; the diff keeps the names. A `Failed` row of the target
check then says which declared name was read as which id. If wrong: a review that names a package or
policy by the new name the same run gives it would fail in the plan and in the first run, as before
this step, or, with a refusal ignored, could reach another object that carries the new name. Since
Sprint 11 step 6 the map holds every declared package, and the rows of an entry that renames nothing
do not speak of a rename: its refusal says the package "has no id in this run", and its note that the
name was read as "the access package its accessPackages entry resolved in this run"
([#review-package-in-the-same-run](#review-package-in-the-same-run)).

**P5 (a review is not registered).** No entry of a document names an access review, so no reader of a
review's rename exists, and the review handler decides through `Resolve-OERStructureRename` without
the map. If wrong: one argument added later.

**P6 (the policy key with the package id).** A policy's outcome is registered under the package's name
and, once the package's id is known, under its id, so a review that names the package by object id
finds the policy's rename; since the rulings recorded in D4 its undecided marks are too. Residual,
accepted, in three places: an entry that stops before it knows any package id -- its catalog refused,
a failed read of the catalog's package list, a package rename that found neither name -- marks its
policies under the name key alone; an entry that stops at a `displayName` several packages of its
catalog carry marks them under those packages' ids, but not under the id of a package that carries
its previous name, which is not looked up by then; and a run whose `-Include` leaves AccessPackages
out marks them under the name key alone (`Invoke-OERStructure` reads nothing for the entry). A review
that names such a package by object id and a policy by its new name then looks the policy up by name
within that package, as before this step: a package the entry could not find or did not reach, or
was not run for. If wrong: one more refusal path.

**D6 (a review renamed).** Both names are looked up in the whole tenant, each the way `displayName`
always is (the same lookup, filter and refusal of a name several definitions carry), the new name
first, so a refusal or a failed read of it returns before the previous name is read. A previous name
that several definitions carry is refused with one `AmbiguousName` record whose target is the
previous name, saying to declare the previous name as the review's object id. An object id is read
once, by id, at `v1.0/identityGovernance/accessReviews/definitions/` followed by the id, with the
not-found codes `NotFound`, `ResourceNotFound` and `Request_ResourceNotFound` declared to the
transport: a not-found answer, or an answer with no object, counts as not matching, and any other
failure is reported `Failed` as itself, with nothing written. The review found, under either name,
passes `Get-OERAccessReviewTargetMismatch` before anything is written to it (`## access-review-target`),
so a review of another package or policy is refused and never renamed, and that row says where the
review was found. The rename is `-DisplayName` in the same `Set-OERAccessReviewDefinition` call as
every other change (a rename alone makes that call), and the definition read back must carry the new
name exactly, letter case included, or the row is `Failed` with a warning; when another field did not
take effect either, the one `Failed` row says both. The decision is made without the map (P5). If
wrong: a review of another package found under its previous name would be renamed, or a rename that
Graph did not store would be reported `Updated`.

**D7 (BL-144; the catalogs handler's reads).** `Sync-OERStructureCatalog` read an existing catalog
with `Get-OERCatalog` and its resources with `Get-OERCatalogResource` without `-ErrorAction Stop`,
and both cmdlets report a failed read as a non-terminating error and return nothing. So, under the
default error preference, a failed catalog read made every declared property look changed and sent
it as a PATCH, and a failed resource read, made after that PATCH, made every declared resource look
absent, so a resource that exists was added again: the defect class of A14 in
`## role-assignment-key`. Both reads now carry `-ErrorAction Stop` and come before the first write
for the entry. A failed read is one `Failed` row that carries the error as itself, written once
through the caller, and says that no catalog update was sent and no resource was added or removed;
nothing else is written for the entry, with `-Prune` as without it, and a `-WhatIf` plan reports the
same row, since the reads are made in a plan too. A catalog read that answers with no object and no
error is a `Failed` row with no error record, as the create's "returned no object" row is. After a
failed read of a catalog that the entry renames, the rename map keeps the decision, as it does after
a failed rename update: the catalog found under its previous name is still the one the document
means. If wrong: a failed read would again be an empty fact that writes.

**The validator and the schema (P4, Rule 14).** `Test-OERStructureSchema` no longer refuses the key on
either kind (`Add-UnsupportedRenameFinding` is deleted) and reads it with the groups' rules: a value
that is not a non-empty string is an Error, and one equal to `displayName` ignoring case is a Warning
naming what makes such a change (`Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy -DisplayName` together with
another property, or `Set-OERAccessReviewDefinition -DisplayName`); for a policy the Warning also
says that the document applies such a change only together with another changed field of the policy
(known limit (e)). A review's previous name is a claim of the accessReviews duplicate check. P4:
among the assignment policies of one package, a `previousDisplayName` is a claim of a new duplicate
check, an Error only when at least one of the two colliding claims is a `previousDisplayName`, naming
the earlier policy by its position in the package; two policies declaring one `displayName` stayed
unreported, as before this step. If wrong: a stricter check is one condition. Sprint 11 step 5 made
that condition: two policies of one package declaring one `displayName` are an Error too, and the
export leaves out every policy whose name another policy of its package carries
([#roster-identity-and-shared-names](#roster-identity-and-shared-names)). Rule 14 has a policy
half: a review whose `assignmentPolicy` equals, ignoring case, the previous name (not an object id)
of a policy the document renames in the package the review names -- by its `displayName`, or by the
name or object id it renames from -- is a Warning, since once the rename is applied no policy of the
package carries the old name and the review's target check fails. The schema declares
`previousDisplayName` on both items as a non-empty string.

**Rule 15 (a package name two entries declare; the controller's ruling on the review of the first
version).** The run's rename map keys a package, and the policies within it, by the package's display
name without its catalog (a policy also by the package's id once the entry knows it), while a package
is identified by its catalog together with its name: two accessPackages entries with one display name
in two catalogs are two packages that share the keys built on that name, so a later entry's mark or
decision would replace an earlier one's, and a review that names the package by that name would reach
whichever entry registered last. `Test-OERStructureSchema` therefore refuses, as an Error at
`accessReviews[i].accessPackage`, a review whose `accessPackage` is a name, not an object id, that two
or more accessPackages entries declare as their `displayName` or as a `previousDisplayName` that
renames -- in this step only while at least one of those entries renamed its package, and since Sprint
11 step 6 (BL-147) whether or not one does, since every accessPackages entry now registers its package
under the name key ([#review-package-in-the-same-run](#review-package-in-the-same-run)); the message
names the entries, names the rename only when one of them renames, and says to name the access
package by its object id. A match on a renaming `previousDisplayName` counts
too: the review's name is then one entry's new name and another entry's old name, and the keys built
on that name are the first entry's, so the review would be read as the first entry's package while it
may mean the other one, which carries the name in the tenant until its rename is applied.
`Invoke-OERStructure` refuses a document that fails validation before it signs in or writes anything.
In this step, when none of those entries renamed its package nothing was reported, and the review's
apply-time lookup refused the ambiguous name: the target check of a review that exists with
`AmbiguousName`, and the create of one that does not with `AmbiguousAccessPackageName`
(`Resolve-OERAccessReviewScopeTarget`), except that a plan for a review that does not exist yet
reached no lookup and said it would create it. Since Sprint 11 step 6 that case is refused offline
too, and the review never reaches a tenant-wide lookup of a name the document declares. No error id
and no schema change. Cost if wrong: a document that was unambiguous to its author -- two same-named
packages in two catalogs -- must name the review's package by its object id.

**Known limits.** (a) A map key joins display names with `|`, so a `|` inside a name can make two keys
collide, and one rename and one review reference are enough to meet it: a package `A|B` whose policy
is renamed to `C` registers the key that a review naming package `A` and policy `B|C` reads, and that
review is then given the id of the policy of `A|B`. A review that exists is checked against that id,
and its target check refuses it when the live review's policy differs. A review that does not exist
yet is created with that id (`Resolve-OERAssignmentPolicyId` takes an object id as given, with no
request), so the create pairs package `A` with a policy of package `A|B`; what Microsoft Graph
answers to such a scope is not measured. And when the decision under that key is a refusal -- a
refused rename or an undecided mark -- the review naming `A` and `B|C` is refused with it, although
it names neither that package nor that policy. A package whose display name is spelled like another
package's object id meets the same three: a review that names that other package by its id reads
the first package's policy keys. (b) Two accessPackages entries with one display name in different
catalogs share the package-name key and the policy keys built on it. Since Sprint 11 step 6 (BL-147)
Rule 15 refuses offline every document in which a review names that name, whether or not one of those
entries renames its package, so an applied document never has a review read a package key two entries
share. A review that names one of those packages by its object id reads only the policy keys built
with that id, which the two entries do not share (P6). (c) A `Rename` registered before a later refusal or failure of the policy
update keeps the id of the policy found under its previous name, so a review in the same run is
checked against that policy while it still carries its old name; step 4 set that precedent for
packages and catalogs. (d) The not-found codes of the access review probe by id (D6): measured live on
2026-10-14 (`docs/live-verification/feat-rename-policies-and-reviews-checklist.md`, 4.3), Microsoft Graph
answers an id that names no review with 404, an EMPTY error code and the message "Fusion batch response 0
returned not found for review" with the id, so the transport derives `NotFound` from the status and the
declared `NotFound` matches; `ResourceNotFound` and `Request_ResourceNotFound` are not what Graph sends
and stay declared only as a margin. A not-found answer under another code still makes the entry
`Failed` with nothing written, the safe direction. The same run measured that a wrapper of
`Invoke-MgGraphRequest` (the checklist's counting proxy, a global function) breaks that path: the
transport's `-StatusCodeVariable` is then set in the wrapper's scope, the status cannot be read, an answer
with an empty code reads as `GraphError` and the entry is `Failed` with the error as itself -- safe, but
not the not-found decision. (e) A rename that
changes the letter case only is not decided through `previousDisplayName` for a policy or a review
either: both names find the one object (for a review, as far as the server's name filter ignores
case, which is not measured), so no rename is decided, and the validator warns. A policy is still
given the declared letter case whenever another declared field of it differs, since the access
package handler sends the declared `displayName` on every update of a policy, and the validator's
warning for a policy says so; a review is given it only by
`Set-OERAccessReviewDefinition -DisplayName`, since the review handler sends `-DisplayName` only for
a rename.

## roster-identity-and-shared-names

Sprint 11 step 5 (BL-131 and BL-142, decision A17) gave every `groupsRoster.json` row the group's
object id and type, counted the names groups share over every group in the tenant, left out the
assignment policies of one access package that share a name, and made the export write a reference
to an object whose name is shared by that object's id. This anchor records the problem, the three
measurements, the rulings with what each costs if it is wrong, the one named deviation from a
single-owner rule, and the known limits. `Get-OERGroupNameIndex` is the single owner of which groups
in the tenant carry a display name, `Get-OERGroupReference` of how the export names a group it
references as a principal, and `Get-OERSharedNameCause` of the cause text, which now carries the
count (CLAUDE.md, Code Style). No ErrorId and no public parameter was added or changed (A9);
`Get-OERGroup`'s output gained three properties, which A17 allows. Apart from measurements A, B and
C, nothing here was measured on its own: the rules were derived from the code and proven with mocked
tests, and the step's live checklist,
`docs/live-verification/feat-roster-identity-and-shared-names-checklist.md`, records the live runs
and names the cases that could not be run live.

**The problem.** Microsoft Entra ID does not keep display names unique, and the apply engine refuses
a name that more than one live object answers to, with nothing written. The export already left out
the objects whose names collided among the objects it read
([#export-group-selection](#export-group-selection), R8), but four gaps remained, and each of the
first three wrote a document that the apply engine refused in part:

1. A group's name was counted among the security-enabled groups the read listed only, so a security
   group that shared its name with a Microsoft 365 group or a distribution group was written, and
   refused when applied.
2. Two assignment policies of one access package that shared a name were both written, and the
   validator left them unreported (Ruling P4 of [#rename-policies-and-reviews](#rename-policies-and-reviews)).
3. A reference was written by name even when the name was shared: an access package's catalog (a
   pair of catalogs of one name that Microsoft Graph no longer lets anyone make, measurement C, but
   that a tenant can still hold from before), an access review's access package or assignment policy
   ([#access-review-target](#access-review-target)), and a group named as the principal of a role
   assignment or a directory role assignment. Each such entry was refused when applied until it was
   edited by hand to an id.
4. `groupsRoster.json` carried names and flags only, so a reader could not tell apart two groups that
   shared a name, nor see which groups were Microsoft 365 or distribution groups.

And the export said that a name was left out, never how many objects carried it.

**Measurement A (the three fields; live, read-only, as `oer-live-cc`, 2026-10-14).** `v1.0/groups`
without `$select` listed 97 groups in the test tenant: 89 security groups, 6 Microsoft 365 groups, 1
distribution group and 1 mail-enabled security group. `mailEnabled` was present and non-null on 97
of 97; `visibility` was present on 97 and non-null on 15 (6 Microsoft 365 groups `Private`, 9 security
groups `Private`), null on the other 82; `createdDateTime` was present and non-null on 97 of 97, and
the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK handed it over as a `[DateTime]`, not a string. So
`ConvertTo-OERGroup` reads all three from the listing the roster already makes, with no `$select` and
no extra request.

**Measurement B (the member count; the same run).** `v1.0/groups/{id}/members/$count` WITHOUT the
`ConsistencyLevel: eventual` header answered `400 Request_UnsupportedQuery` on every group tried.
WITH it, the count equalled the full read -- the member list joined with its
`microsoft.graph.servicePrincipal` cast -- on the five groups read (0, 1, 1, 2 and 5 members), and so
did the inline `$count=true&$top=1`; the `$count` body arrives as a string. No group in the test
tenant had a service principal as a member (97 reads), so the two open parts were measured in this
step's live checklist, `docs/live-verification/feat-roster-identity-and-shared-names-checklist.md`
(checks 1.2 and 1.3; live, the test tenant, `oer-live-cc`, 2026-10-14), with prefixed objects.
A service principal (1.2): a security group whose only member was a service principal listed 0
members with the v1.0 member list, which leaves the service principal out, 1 with the
`microsoft.graph.servicePrincipal` cast and 1 in the module's full read, which joins the two;
`members/$count` with `ConsistencyLevel: eventual` answered 1, so it counts the service principal
and equals the full read, and without the header it answered `400 Request_UnsupportedQuery`. Right
after a change (1.3): a second member was added to a group and removed again. After the add, both
reads still showed the old count at once; the eventual count showed the new one at 6 s, the full read
only at 16 s. After the remove both showed the old count at once and the new one at 6 s. So in this
tenant the eventual count trailed a change no more than the full read did; both trail by seconds.
Decision, unchanged: no member count for every group in this step -- it would cost a request per
group, and the module's single Graph transport cannot send the header
([#export-group-selection](#export-group-selection), R3).

**Measurement C (catalog names; live, the test tenant, `oer-live-cc`, 2026-10-14, check 0.2 of the
same checklist).** Microsoft Graph refuses to create a catalog whose name another catalog carries,
letter case aside (`400 DuplicateCatalog`, for the exact name and for a name differing only in
letter case), and refuses to rename a catalog to such a name (`409 DuplicateKey`). So two catalogs
that share a name cannot be made today; a tenant may still hold such a pair from before this refusal
(not measured). BL-39's twin-catalog case (a package written with its catalog's id, R-5) is
therefore proved offline only (the checklist's B.8), and the guard that fails a package re-created
into another catalog was proved live on the older case: a package declared in a uniquely named
catalog while a package of the same name exists in another catalog (check 3.5, one `Failed` row,
nothing written).

**R-1 (the roster shape).** `ConvertTo-OERGroup`, the single owner of the group shape, gains
`MailEnabled` (after `SecurityEnabled`), `Visibility` and `CreatedDateTime` (last). A boolean
`mailEnabled` is carried as itself and anything else as empty; the visibility as given, or empty; the
creation time as one UTC ISO 8601 string (`yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ`) whatever form it arrives in -- a
`[DateTime]` (measured), a `[DateTimeOffset]` or the string -- with a `[DateTime]` of unspecified kind
taken as UTC and never converted from local time, and an unreadable value empty, never an error.
Each roster row keeps its five keys and gains, after them, `id`, `securityEnabled`, `mailEnabled`,
`groupTypes` (always an array of strings, empty for a group that is neither a Microsoft 365 group nor
dynamic), `visibility` and `createdDateTime`, read from the converted object and never from the raw
response. `inventory.json` stays without an id key on its entries. Cost if wrong: the roster reads
three raw fields itself, and `Get-OERGroup` does not show them.

**R-1b (the table view).** The Group table view keeps its four columns, and the new properties show
with `Format-List` or `Select-Object *`: seven columns no longer fit a console. Cost if wrong: one more
column in the view.

**R-2 (one index of every group's name, one rule for a group reference).** `Get-OERGroupNameIndex`
builds the index from the groups it is given (`-Group`, the export's roster, with no request) or
from ONE paged listing `v1.0/groups?$select=id,displayName&$top=999`, which `Get-OERInventory` makes
at most once per invocation -- when its Groups section read at least one group, or when a section
holds a group principal whose name was read -- and shares between them. It keys a name without regard to letter case,
the key the validator refuses a duplicate on, and lists each group's id once, lower-cased. A failed
listing comes back as `Read` false with its message: never thrown, and never an empty index.
`Get-OERGroupReference` writes a group's display name only when the index was read and exactly this
group carries that name, and the object id otherwise -- an index not read, a blank name, a name the
index lists under another group or under several -- which the apply engine resolves verbatim. A
group principal whose name is blank, or is its id because its name could not be read, is written by
its id without reading the listing, since the rule returns the id for it whatever the index holds.
One listing per invocation was chosen over a lookup per name. Cost if wrong, and it multiplies:
`Export-OERInventory` calls `Get-OERInventory` once per Azure scope it walks, and a scope's role
assignment read returns the assignments inherited from above it too, so one group assignment at a
management group makes every scope beneath it list every group once -- ceil(G/999) Graph requests
per such scope for G groups in the tenant, for example about 9,300 requests for 300 scopes and
30,000 groups. A listing that fails costs no more than its own requests: the group principals of
that invocation are written by id (R-3c). A lookup per name was considered and costs the same
order: k names per scope, an inherited name looked up again at every scope beneath its assignment.
The controller raises the multiplier to the architect. Closed for the export in Sprint 11 step 6: an
export shares one index among all its calls ([#export-run-context](#export-run-context)).

**R-3 (the counts reach the export).** `Get-OERInventory` hands every name it left out, with its
section and count, to its caller in ONE information record tagged `Omnicit.EntraRBAC.SharedName` (a
`Names` list of `Section`, `Name` and `Count`), the pattern of the root-scope record
([#root-scope-is-not-in-the-document](#root-scope-is-not-in-the-document)), and the group reader
returns its own in a new `SharedNames` list. `Export-OERInventory` collects the record with
`-InformationVariable` under `-InformationAction SilentlyContinue`, joins the reader's names first and
`Get-OERInventory`'s after, writes ONE warning before its `ShouldProcess`, and hands the names to the
bundle README, whose section "Names two or more objects share" follows "Role assignments at the root
scope (elevated access)". The names stay in `IncompleteReads` as before. No public parameter and no
hidden channel. Cost if wrong: an information record a caller sees with `-InformationAction Continue`.

**R-3b (a review reference is checked with the apply engine's own lookups).** A review's
`accessPackage` or `assignmentPolicy` name stays only when the lookup the apply engine makes for it
finds exactly that object: the access package name in the whole tenant (`Resolve-OERAccessPackageId`'s
URI, the name escaped the same way), the assignment policy name among the policies of the review's
access package (`Resolve-OERAssignmentPolicyId`'s listing, compared as it compares). Otherwise the id
is written and nothing is reported, since the id applies. Each answer is cached for the invocation,
so the reviews of one access package cost one lookup of each kind however many there are: one request
per access package name and one per access package. A lookup that fails writes the id too and is
reported like a failed name read -- the cause, and the review's `accessPackage` or `assignmentPolicy`
named unread under `accessReviews` -- since an id otherwise reads as a deleted target. Cost if wrong:
up to two extra requests per distinct package.

**The named deviation (the controller's ruling on the review of Task 3b).** CLAUDE.md makes
`Resolve-OERAssignmentPolicyId` the single owner of the assignment policy name lookup, and
`Resolve-OERAccessPackageId` resolves an access package name. `Get-OERInventory` sends the two lookups
itself instead of calling the resolvers, which throw `AmbiguousName` for a shared name -- the very
case the check exists for -- and would leave stray records in a caller's `-ErrorVariable`, the reason
the review's name read is a transport read too. The Context "the export's review-reference lookups
agree with the resolvers (named deviation)" in `tests/Unit/Public/Get-OERInventory.Tests.ps1` drives
the resolvers and the export's lookups under one mock and asserts the same URIs and the same
decisions for a unique name, a shared one, none and another object. CLAUDE.md names it as the one
exception to its bullet. Cost if wrong: two copies of a lookup that only a test keeps in step.

**R-3c (an index that could not be read).** When the listing of every group fails, every group
principal is written by its object id -- an exact reference the apply engine resolves verbatim -- so
nothing is missing from the document and no group principal is reported unread; the verbose stream
says so once per invocation. The Groups section, which counts names, reports `groupNames` unread
with the cause instead and counts the names among the groups it read. Cost if wrong: an export whose
group principals are all ids, with only a verbose line saying why.

**R-3d (what the README lists).** The README lists the names LEFT OUT of a section -- groups,
administrative units, catalogs, the access packages of one catalog, access reviews and the
assignment policies of one access package -- one bullet per name, with how many objects carry it and
its section. A reference written as an id is explained in the section's introduction and in the
prompt, not listed per name. Cost if wrong: the reader cannot see which reference ids stand for
shared names.

**R-3e (the warning's numbers).** The export's one warning gives how many names were left out and
how many objects carry them in all, over every section, a group's name counted over the whole
tenant, Microsoft 365 and distribution groups included. Cost if wrong: a number that includes
namesakes never in `inventory.json`'s scope.

**R-4 (texts that carry the controller's numbers).** Task 4, measurement B written into R3 of
[#export-group-selection](#export-group-selection), was batched with the texts of Task 5 into one
dispatch, and the outcome of the live checklist (measurements B and C) was added after the live run by
a small follow-up: both are texts that carry numbers only the controller holds. Cost if wrong: none beyond one batched
review.

**R-5 (a package's catalog, and `-Catalog`).** An access package whose catalog's name another
catalog the export read carries is written with the catalog's object id, which the apply engine takes
as the catalog itself (`Resolve-OERCatalogId` returns a GUID as given), so access packages of one
name in two such catalogs are two entries and not a collision; the unread paths of such a catalog
name it the same way. The catalogs themselves are left out as before. The names are counted over the
catalogs the export read, with no extra lookup: `-Catalog` given as an id reads that catalog alone,
so a package in it keeps the catalog's name even when another catalog in the tenant carries it, and
given as a name it reads every catalog Microsoft Graph matches by that name, which are counted. Such
a pair of catalogs can be held only by a tenant that made it before Microsoft Graph refused to create
or rename a catalog to a name another carries (measurement C), so the rule serves those tenants and
has no live case in the test tenant. Cost if wrong: a package in a filtered catalog whose name another catalog shares is written by name and
refused when applied (`AmbiguousName`, nothing written).

**R-6 (what this step does not cover).** A group named as a PIM for Groups eligibility principal, as
an access review's reviewer, or as a catalog resource or an access package resource role keeps its
display name: none of these positions has a `principalType` key, and A17 names a group as a
principal, with `principalType` `Group`. They are reported as findings outside this step's scope.
Cost if wrong: those positions still write a shared group name, which the apply engine refuses
(`AmbiguousName`, nothing written).

**The validator and the policies of one package (Task 3a).** `Test-OERStructureSchema` drops the
exception of Ruling P4: two assignment policies of one access package that claim one name are an
Error whatever the two claims are -- two `displayName`s, a `displayName` and a `previousDisplayName`,
or two `previousDisplayName`s -- at the later claim's path, naming the earlier policy by its position;
the same name in two packages is two policies. The export leaves out every policy whose name another
policy of its package carries, letter case aside, and reports the name once with its count, named
`accessPackages/` followed by the package name, `/assignmentPolicies/` and the policy name (section
`assignmentPolicies`, reported as `<package>/<policy>`); the policies of two packages never count
against each other. Leaving a policy out removes nothing, since the apply engine never removes an
assignment policy. Cost if wrong: a document an earlier version exported that holds such a pair is
now refused whole by the offline check, where before only that policy's entry was refused when
applied.

**The widened filter (the controller's ruling on Task 2).** A security group whose name a group
carries that a widened `-GroupFilter` listed and `-SecurityEnabledOnly` dropped -- a group that is not
security-enabled -- is left out when the roster was read, since the index holds every group in the
tenant. That overrides, for the count only, the rule of R5 and R6 of
[#export-group-selection](#export-group-selection) that a dropped group is out of scope before the
shared names are counted: A17 counts shared names over every group, and the apply engine would refuse
the name anyway. When the roster could not be read, the rule holds as before. Cost if wrong: one
security group fewer in `inventory.json`, named in `IncompleteReads` and the README.

**Root-scope rows (the controller's ruling on Task 3c).** A role assignment row passes the group rule
of R-2 before the root-scope split
([#root-scope-is-not-in-the-document](#root-scope-is-not-in-the-document)), so two root-scope groups
that share a name are named by id in the warning, the information record and the README list: one
reference rule for every row the section reads. Cost if wrong: a root-scope finding names a group by
its id instead of its shared name.

**Known limits.** (a) `-Catalog` given as an id (R-5) and the positions R-6 leaves out still write a
shared name, refused when applied. (b) A display name of an access package or an assignment policy
that is shaped like a GUID is read by the apply engine as an object id, and the export can keep such
a name in a review, where the engine then reads it as an id and not as the name; very improbable. (c) Closed in this
step (the controller's ruling on the final review): `New-OERAccessPackage` looks a package up by name
in the whole tenant, so re-creating a package declared in catalog A while exactly one package of that
name exists in catalog B returned B's package, and `Sync-OERStructureAccessPackage` reported it
`Created` and went on to write the declared resource roles and assignment policies to it. The gap is
older than this step, for every catalog named uniquely; the catalog id written here let it reach a
package whose catalog's name is shared (refused as ambiguous before), a pair only a tenant from
before Microsoft Graph's refusal can hold (measurement C). The handler now compares the
catalog of the package `New-OERAccessPackage` returns with the declared catalog, as ids without
regard to letter case -- an id as written, a name looked up once with `Resolve-OERCatalogId` -- and
when they differ reports the entry as one `Failed` row and returns, with nothing written to that
package or for the entry; a lookup that fails is scrubbed first and reported `Failed` with its error,
nothing further written. A package with no catalog in the answer is one the create sent into the
declared catalog whose confirmation read did not answer, and is reported `Created` as before. No
ErrorId was added. Residual: none. (d) `Get-OERInventory` reads the listing of every group once per
invocation that meets a group principal whose name was read, and `Export-OERInventory` makes one
invocation per Azure scope, whose role assignment read returns inherited assignments too: one group
assignment at a management group costs ceil(G/999) requests at every scope beneath it (about 9,300
for 300 scopes and 30,000 groups, R-2), raised to the architect; a lookup per name costs the same
order. Closed for the export in Sprint 11 step 6: `Export-OERInventory` shares ONE index among all
its `Get-OERInventory` calls, the roster's when the roster was read and otherwise the first caller's
listing, so an export lists every group at most once
([#export-run-context](#export-run-context)); a standalone `Get-OERInventory` still lists at most
once per invocation. A group row at the root scope alone makes `Get-OERInventory` read the listing, and the
verbose line of R-3c says "every group principal" even when only root-scope rows met it. (e) The policies of a
package that is itself left out for a shared name are still reported, and two same-named packages of
one catalog that each hold a same-named pair of policies report the policy name twice, the same way:
noise, since neither package is written. (f) Closed by the live checklist (measurement B): `$count` counts a
service principal, and it trails a membership change by seconds, as the full read does.

**Since Sprint 11 step 6.** `principalType` is written for every `roleAssignments` row whose principal
type maps to the schema enum, a group written by its name included, so the collision pass no longer
stamps it ([#unresolved-principals](#unresolved-principals)). A group principal that the directory did
not return, or whose lookup failed, carries its object id as its name, which `Get-OERGroupReference`
returns as it is, with no index read.

### Sprint 11 step 10: names and the order of reads in Get-OERInventory (BL-156, BL-45, BL-24; R-10, R-11)

**BL-156 and R-10 (a shared name is a cause of its own).** `Format-OERUnreadCauseClause` deduplicates the
causes of an `InventoryPartial` message on a key: the message with its `Target` -- the failing object's own
id, taken from its record -- replaced by `<id>`, so that seven units that fail for one reason are one cause.
A shared-name cause was registered with the name's own unread entry as its `Target` (`groups/Admins`), and
`Get-OERSharedNameCause` writes that entry into its text, so the replacement turned every name of one count
into the same key (`2 live objects share the name <id> (compared ...`), and the clause kept the first name
only. That happened in `Get-OERInventory`'s `Select-UniqueNamedEntry` and in the group clause of
`Export-OERInventory`, which formats the causes `Get-OERInventoryGroup -ExcludeSharedName` returns. The unread
entries and the README still named every name; only the causes clause lost one, so an operator reading the
message saw one name where two were left out. Both sites now register the cause with a BLANK `Target`, which
the clause reads as "no id to normalise", so the key is the full text: each name is a cause of its own, and one
name is still stated once however many objects carry it. `Format-OERUnreadCauseClause` and the id
normalisation of every other cause are unchanged. The cost is length: a tenant with many shared names states
each, and the cap of 23 distinct causes can drop a shared-name cause like any other, and says how many it
dropped; the unread keys stay and the verbose stream carries every one. Where a shared-name cause stands in
that order depends on the call: the group reader and the five calls `Get-OERInventory` makes once every section
is read add theirs after the other causes, so the cap drops those first, while the assignment policies' call
adds its causes as each access package is read, ahead of the causes of the sections read after it. Cost if
wrong: put the
`Target` back, and a second name of one count disappears from the clause again.

**BL-45 (a role name of white space).** A role assignment's `role` and a directory role entry's `role` fell
back to the role definition id only when the name was empty or missing, so a name of spaces was written as
it was, and the validator refuses an empty name and cannot tell white space from one. Both now use
`[string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace` on the name and fall back to the id the row already carries, the rule the
administrative unit's scoped role line already has. The duplicate schedule warning of the directory
section names the role the same way, so the warning and the entry it is about agree. A name that is not blank
is written as it is. Cost if wrong: a role whose name is white space is written as that white space again.

**BL-24 and R-11 (the package list is read before the catalog resources).** The AccessPackages section read
each catalog's resources first, only to name the bindings of the packages it listed next, and sent that read
for a catalog that holds no package at all, and for one whose package list then failed, naming
`accessPackages/<catalog>/catalogResourceNames` unread for a read nothing needed. It now reads the package
list first and reads the catalog's resources, and asks `Resolve-OERPrincipalName` for the group and
application names through the shared name map, only for a catalog whose list was read and holds a package: a
catalog with none has no binding to name, and a failed list is already named unread as
`accessPackages/<catalog>/packages`, with no resource read behind it. A failed resource read of a catalog that
does hold a package is named as before. The Catalogs section reads a catalog's resources for the catalog's own
entry, separately, and is not changed; the shared name map is still filled by whichever section needs it
first. A failed package list now names `packages` alone for its catalog, since a failed list reads no
resources, so a catalog's `packages` and `catalogResourceNames` entries can no longer both be named, and no
other entry changes. Cost if wrong: one resource read more per catalog that holds no package, and a
`catalogResourceNames` entry for a read that was never needed.

### Sprint 11 step 11: a name or a scope id of white space (BL-157)

**Fourth point: names.** BL-45 fixed the role names of the role assignment and directory role
sections; three more projections still tested a name for truth, so a name of spaces was written as it
was. `ConvertTo-OERInventoryRoleManagementPolicy` (the `role` of a `roleManagementPolicies` and a
`directoryRoleManagementPolicies` entry) and `Get-OERInventoryAzureEligibility` (the `role` and
`principal` of an `azurePimEligibility.json` row) now use `[string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace` and fall back
to the role definition id or the principal id, each on its own, as BL-45 does. A name that is not
blank is written as it is, surrounding white space included.

**Fifth point: scope ids.** `Resolve-OERInventoryScopeTree` added a listed management group or
subscription to the walk's scope list when its `ResourceId` was truthy, so a `ResourceId` of white
space was walked as a scope and counted in the export's "N of M Azure scopes could not be read". It
now uses `[string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace`, as it already did for an empty or missing id, so such a
scope is neither walked nor counted.

**The named limit (ruled in the step).** A listed subscription or management group with a blank
`ResourceId` is therefore in the hierarchy (`scopeHierarchy.json`) but neither walked nor counted,
and nothing names it unread, even when the subscription decides as the session tenant's own (the
home tenant check falls back to `/subscriptions/<id>` for its verdict). Azure Resource Manager's
answer always carries the id (`ConvertTo-OERSubscription` takes `ResourceId` from it), and an empty
or missing id already behaved this way, so the edge is defensive; walking such a subscription by its
`SubscriptionId`, or naming it unread, is a behaviour choice left to a later step. Cost if wrong: such
a subscription is not walked and not named unread.

### CLAUDE.md text for roster-identity-and-shared-names

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Get-OERGroupNameIndex` is the single owner of which groups in the tenant carry a display
  name**: from the groups given (`-Group`, the export's roster) with no request, or from ONE paged
  listing `v1.0/groups?$select=id,displayName&$top=999`, which `Get-OERInventory` reads at most once
  per invocation, and `Export-OERInventory` at most once per export through its run context (below).
  It never throws and never writes an error record: it returns `Read`, `IdsByName`
  (a name, compared without regard to letter case, to the lower-cased ids that carry it; `$null` when
  the listing failed, never an empty index) and `Message`. **`Get-OERGroupReference` is the single
  owner of how the export names a group it references as the principal of a role assignment or a
  directory role assignment**: its display name only when the index was read and exactly this group
  carries the name; otherwise its object id, written with `principalType` `Group` in
  `roleAssignments` and `directoryRoleAssignments`. A group named as an eligibility principal, a
  reviewer, a catalog resource or a resource role is outside it and keeps its display name (R-6).
  Never re-implement either inline.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#roster-identity-and-shared-names`

## measured-not-found-codes

Sprint 11 step 10 (BL-21, R-13): the not-found codes of two reads are the ones measured. This anchor records
which code each read declares and why it declares no other.
