**The problem (BL-21).** `Get-OERAccessReviewInstance -Instance` sorted a failed single-instance GET as a
missing instance when the converted error id was one of four codes (`ResourceNotFound`,
`Request_ResourceNotFound`, `ItemNotFound` and `NotFound`), and the catalog list read of `Get-OERInventory`
carried a copy of the same four for a by-id `-Catalog` read, beside `CatalogNotFound`. Both lists were declared
while the real code was unknown, a superset that is a guess (the same shape `Resolve-OERAccessPackageId`
dropped for the access package probe), and an unobserved code is as likely to mean something else as to mean
"missing".

**What was measured (2026-10-19, read-only, as the dedicated live-verification identity, through the module's
transport).** A missing access review definition, the instance list of a missing definition, and a missing
instance of a missing definition or of an existing one: Microsoft Graph answers 404 with NO error code in the
body, so the id the module carries is the status-derived `NotFound`. A catalog by a missing id: 404 with the
code `CatalogNotFound`, which `Get-OERCatalog -Id` republishes as `CatalogNotFound`.

**R-13 (the instance read).** The single-instance GET declares `-ExpectedErrorCode 'NotFound'` and turns the
`Omnicit.EntraRBAC.GraphExpectedError` marker it gets back into the existing `AccessReviewInstanceNotFound`,
with the message, category and target it always had and no inner exception, since the marker is an answer and
nothing was raised. Every other failure is scrubbed and published as itself, and the four-code list is gone, so
`ResourceNotFound`, `Request_ResourceNotFound` and `ItemNotFound` are no longer read as a missing instance. The
transport compares whole tokens and reads a failure's message text only when its id is status-derived, so a 403
that carries a real code is never softened into "not found" by prose such as "the caller does not have access
to the resource, or it does not exist". **The catalog by-id list** keeps its `CatalogNotFound*` and
`AmbiguousCatalogName*` arms, which republish the record as itself and count nothing unread, and loses the
four-code segment test: a by-id failure that carries one of the four is a catalog list that could not be read,
named unread (`catalogs` and `accessPackages`) with its cause, the safe direction to be wrong in. Cost if
wrong: a Graph that answers one of those endpoints with a code the module does not declare makes the instance
read publish that error as itself instead of the friendly id, and the catalog by-id read name the catalogs
unread instead of republishing the not-found record, each repaired by adding the one measured code to the
declaration or to the arm.

## export-run-context

Sprint 11 step 6 (R-2 of step 5, ruling R-1, amended on the review of Task 1) gave one export a
context that all its `Get-OERInventory` calls share. This anchor records why it exists, why it is a
module-scope object keyed on the export's own invocation rather than a parameter, why there is no
`try`/`finally` around it, and its limits. No public parameter was added (A9). The rules were
derived from the code and proven with mocked tests; nothing here was measured live.

**The problem.** `Export-OERInventory` calls `Get-OERInventory` once for the Entra ID sections and
once per Azure scope it walks, and every call was standalone. Each call that met a group principal
listed every group in the tenant again ([#roster-identity-and-shared-names](#roster-identity-and-shared-names),
R-2 and known limit (d): about 9,300 requests for 300 scopes and 30,000 groups), and what one call
learned about a role assignment principal could neither be shared with the next scope nor handed
back to the export, short of a new public parameter.

**R-1 (one object, one creator).** `Export-OERInventory` creates `$script:_OERInventoryRunContext` in
ONE place, directly before its Entra ID `Get-OERInventory` call, overwriting whatever stood there, and
sets it back to `$null` with a plain statement directly after the Azure walk. Its members:

- `Owner`: the export's own `$MyInvocation`;
- `GroupNameIndex`: the `Get-OERGroupNameIndex` result -- the index built from the roster when the
  roster was read, with no request, and otherwise `$null` until the first caller lists every group
  once and stores the index there;
- `PrincipalStatus`: a dictionary, keyed without regard to letter case, of every answer of the
  deleted items read that succeeded, so a principal whose read succeeds is read once per export; a
  read that fails is not kept, and the next scope that needs it reads again
  ([#unresolved-principals](#unresolved-principals));
- `UnreadPrincipal` and `UnreadPrincipalCause`: the role assignment principals that could not be
  read, and their causes, index for index, which the export names in `IncompleteReads` and its own
  `InventoryPartial` -- without the entries of a scope it skipped, and without a failed lookup of an
  assignment that another scope read (known limits (b) and (e) of
  [#unresolved-principals](#unresolved-principals));
- `SubscriptionTenant` (added in Sprint 11 step 8, A20, BL-152): a dictionary, keyed without regard to
  letter case, of what the export's scope tree learned about each subscription -- the facts the
  subscription list gave, with no request, and a `-Scope`'s one read -- which
  `Get-OERSubscriptionHomeTenant -Cache` stores and reads, so the export's per-scope `Get-OERInventory`
  calls decide a subscription's home tenant with no request
  ([#home-tenant-subscriptions](#home-tenant-subscriptions)). It is the one member only the owner
  writes: the export hands it to `Resolve-OERInventoryScopeTree -Cache`, `Get-OERInventory` hands it
  to its own owner calls, and the owner stores there what a read or the list gave. A context without
  it, a test fixture's for one, reads as none, and `Get-OERInventory` then keeps a cache of its own for
  the invocation;
- `PrincipalNameCache` (added in Sprint 11 step 10, BL-122, R-12; third in the object, after
  `GroupNameIndex`): the id to display name hashtable the export creates before its group read, hands to
  `Get-OERInventoryGroup -PrincipalNameCache` and puts here, the very same object in all three places.
  See the paragraph on it below.

A local reference keeps the two lists after the context is cleared. Cost if wrong: one more member for
each thing an export shares; the alternative, a parameter, would have been a new public parameter.

**The cache of principal names (Sprint 11 step 10, BL-122, R-12).** The group reader names the principals of
a group's PIM eligibility through `Resolve-OERPrincipalName` into an id to display name cache, and
`Get-OERInventory` names the reviewers of an access review and the principals of a directory role section
through another, so a principal that stands in both -- a user who is eligible for a group and also reviews
an access review -- was looked up twice per export. The reader has always taken its cache as a parameter
(`-PrincipalNameCache`), which `Get-OERInventory`'s own Groups section passes, so the export only had to hand
the reader a hashtable it also keeps: `Export-OERInventory` creates it before its group read (an export that
reads no Groups section leaves it empty, which is what the call used to start from), passes it to the reader
and puts it in the context as `PrincipalNameCache`. `Get-OERInventory` takes it as its own
`$PrincipalNameCache` right after it has decided that the context is its own (the owner check below), and
before the Groups section reads, so what the reader learned is found by the reviewers and the directory
role section, and what this call learns stays for the calls after it. The member is read through
`PSObject.Properties`, as `SubscriptionTenant` is, and used only when it is a `[hashtable]` (R-27): the
consumers need one. `Get-OERInventoryGroup -PrincipalNameCache` is a `[hashtable]` parameter, which binds any
other dictionary as a COPY, so what the reader learned would be lost to the call without an error, and the
sections below call `ContainsKey`, which an `[ordered]` dictionary has not, so the reviewers and the directory
role sections would throw. R-12 first copied the `IDictionary` test of the `SubscriptionTenant` member, whose
consumer (`Get-OERSubscriptionHomeTenant -Cache`) is an `IDictionary` parameter; this member's consumers are
not. A context without the member, or with one that is no `[hashtable]`, reads as none, and the call keeps
the hashtable it made at the top of its `process` block, which it always did. A call that has no context of
its own -- a standalone one, or one that finds a stale context -- uses that hashtable and leaves the stale
one alone. The
tests hold the same object in the reader and the context (`ReferenceEquals`), the lookups counted
(`Resolve-OERPrincipalName` is not called for a principal the reader named, and once for one it did not),
and the six readings of a context that has no usable member (missing, null, a string, an array, an
`[ordered]` dictionary and a generic dictionary). Known limit: `Resolve-OERPrincipalName`'s map answers an id
the directory did not return, and every id of a batch whose request failed, with the id itself, and the
cache keeps that answer like any other, so a lookup that failed in the group read is not retried by the
Entra ID call, which writes the id it would have written after a second failure. Cost if wrong: one lookup
more for each principal both name, as before, and a hashtable that lives for one export. A test that builds
a context by hand needs no new member: without it the call keeps its own cache.

**The owner check.** `Get-OERInventory` reads the context ONCE per invocation and uses it only when its
`Owner` is the `InvocationInfo` of a frame of the current call stack, compared by reference through
`Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Get-PSCallStack` -- module-qualified, as `Lock-OERSignIn` calls it, so a
session function of that name cannot turn the check off. That the export's `$MyInvocation` IS the
object its call stack frame carries was measured with the tests: an owner stored as
`$MyInvocation.MyCommand` instead matches no frame and turns six of them red. Otherwise the call
behaves exactly as standalone, with a holder of its own that nothing outlives. So a context an export
leaves behind when it is stopped before the clearing statement is ignored by every later call, a
later export's included, which overwrites it.

**No `try`/`finally` (the controller's ruling on Task 1).** The first version cleared the context in a
`finally` around the region. Measured in a scratch `pwsh`: without a `try`, a statement-terminating
error (`$X = Thrower`, where `Thrower` calls `ThrowTerminatingError`) skips that statement and the
function carries on; inside `try { } finally { }` it skips the REST of the `try` body -- here the
whole Azure walk -- runs the `finally` and carries on after it. So the `finally` would have changed the
export's control flow, and the owner check replaced it. A test holds that a statement-terminating
error in the Entra ID call still skips only that statement, and that the walk runs and the bundle is
written. It runs the export in a runspace of its own, from a script with no `try`, because every test
body runs inside a `try` that Pester itself wraps around it, and there such an error would be caught
by Pester's `try` up the call stack instead of skipping only its own statement.

**Known limits.** (a) A stopped export's context keeps its `InvocationInfo`, and with it the export's
bound parameters, a tenant among them, until the next export overwrites it or the module is removed.
It holds no token, and nothing reads it once its owner is off the stack. (b) A listing of every group
that fails is kept in the context for the whole export, as it was kept for one call before, so the
export does not retry it at the next scope: the group principals of every scope are then written by
object id, which is exact and leaves nothing unread, and the verbose line of R-3c of
[#roster-identity-and-shared-names](#roster-identity-and-shared-names) repeats once per scope.
(c) The owner check's `$null -ne Owner` term is an equivalent guard: no frame carries a null
`InvocationInfo`, so a context without an owner matches nothing either way. It stays as a defence.

### CLAUDE.md text for export-run-context

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Export-OERInventory` is the only command that sets and clears the export run context
  (`$script:_OERInventoryRunContext`)**, the one object its `Get-OERInventory` calls share (the
  group name index, the principal names the group read looked up, `PrincipalNameCache`, the deleted
  items answers, the role assignment principals that could not be read, and the subscription home
  tenant answers, `SubscriptionTenant`);
  `Get-OERInventory` fills its members, `Get-OERDeletedPrincipalStatus` through the `PrincipalStatus`
  dictionary it is handed, except `SubscriptionTenant`, which the export hands to
  `Resolve-OERInventoryScopeTree -Cache` and `Get-OERInventory` to the owner the same way, so
  `Get-OERSubscriptionHomeTenant -Cache` is what fills it (a context without the member reads as
  none). Export creates it in ONE place, directly before its Entra ID
  `Get-OERInventory` call, with `Owner` set to its own `$MyInvocation`, and sets it back to `$null`
  with a plain statement directly after the Azure walk -- never in a `finally`, which turns a
  statement-terminating error into a skip of the rest of the walk. `Get-OERInventory` reads it once
  per invocation and uses it only while its `Owner` is the `InvocationInfo` of a frame of the current
  call stack (`Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Get-PSCallStack`, compared by reference), and behaves
  standalone otherwise, so a context a stopped export left behind is ignored. Never read or write it
  anywhere else, never replace it by a public parameter (A9), and add a member to it rather than a
  second module variable. `PrincipalNameCache` (Sprint 11 step 10, BL-122) is a `[hashtable]`, id to
  name, that the export creates before its group read and hands, the very same object, to
  `Get-OERInventoryGroup -PrincipalNameCache` and to the context, so a principal the group read named
  is not looked up again by the Entra ID call; `Get-OERInventory` takes it, read through
  `PSObject.Properties` as `SubscriptionTenant` is, only when the context is its own and the member
  is a `[hashtable]` (its consumers bind one and call `ContainsKey`), and keeps its own otherwise.
  Known limit: a lookup that failed in the group read is not retried, since the map
  `Resolve-OERPrincipalName` returns answers the id as the name.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#export-run-context`

## unresolved-principals

Sprint 11 step 6 (BL-133, decision A18) made the export tell a role assignment principal the directory
did not return from one it could not look up, and made the apply engine never create a role
assignment for the first. This anchor records the problem, the measurement, the rulings with what
each costs if it is wrong, and the known limits. `Get-OERDeletedPrincipalStatus` is the one read of
`directory/deletedItems` (CLAUDE.md, Code Style). No ErrorId and no public parameter was added (A9).

**The problem (BL-133).** `Get-OERInventory` named a role assignment's principal through
`Resolve-OERPrincipalName`, whose map falls back to the object id both for an id the directory did not
return and for every id of a batch whose request failed. A deleted principal, a principal of another
tenant (Azure Lighthouse, say) and a failed lookup therefore all came out as the same bare object id,
with nothing to tell them apart: a failed read was written as if it were a fact, and nothing in the
document told the apply engine that the principal was not a live object.

**The measurement (live, read-only, as `oer-live-cc`, 2026-10-15).** A read of
`v1.0/directory/deletedItems/{id}` for an id the directory holds nowhere answered 404 with the error
code `Request_ResourceNotFound`, and the deleted items collections of users, groups and service
principals answered 200. So the read by id needs no object type, and `Request_ResourceNotFound` is the
not-found code; `ResourceNotFound` and `NotFound` are declared beside it as a margin only. A read by
the id of an object that IS among the deleted items was not measured in this step: the `Deleted`
answer rests on the documented read ("Get deleted item (directory object)", Microsoft Learn).

**R-2 (the lookup).** `Resolve-OERPrincipalName -Detailed` omits the getByIds `types` filter, so every
directory object type is searched, and returns one object per distinct id: `Id`, `Read`, `Found`,
`Name`, `ObjectType` and `Cause`. `Read` is false, with the cause, for every id of a batch whose request
failed, and (fix round 1, F5) of a batch whose answer carries no `value` collection, which says
nothing about its ids; an empty `value` IS an answer. `Found` true carries the name (a user's user
principal name, else the display name, else the id) and the object type. `Read` true and `Found` false
is an id a successful batch did not return. Without `-Detailed` the map is exactly what it was for its
other callers. Sprint 11 step 8 (its Ruling R-8) added two properties to the `-Detailed` answer,
`DisplayName` and `UserPrincipalName`, after `ObjectType` (each `$null` when blank, not found or not
read; `Name` and its rule unchanged), and two callers of `-Detailed` that read no deleted items: the
`administrativeUnits` scoped role type lookup ([#scoped-role-principal-type](#scoped-role-principal-type))
and `Get-OERServicePrincipalAccess`, for the users named in delegated permission grants
([#service-principal-access](#service-principal-access)). So the `roleAssignments` section is still
the only one that reads the deleted items, but no longer the only caller of `-Detailed`.
`Get-OERDeletedPrincipalStatus` reads `v1.0/directory/deletedItems/{id}`, the id
escaped, with the three not-found codes declared to the transport: an object is `Deleted`; the
not-found marker is `Unresolved`, read; a throw (scrubbed first) or an empty answer is `Unresolved`,
NOT read, with its cause. It never throws and never writes an error record, and keeps an answer that
was read under the lower-cased id in the dictionary it is handed, never a failure. Microsoft Learn's
page for that read asks for a permission per object type (`User.Read.All`, `Group.Read.All`,
`Application.Read.All`), and the type is not known before the read, so `Directory.Read.All`, which the
inventory already requires, is the one permission that covers it; `tests/QA/requiredscope.tests.ps1`
holds a read of the path to `Directory.Read.All` or `Directory.ReadWrite.All`, and a write to
`Directory.ReadWrite.All`. Cost if wrong: one request per principal not returned, once per export
while the read succeeds; a read that fails is sent again by the next scope that needs it.

**R-3 (what the export writes).**

- **A failed lookup.** The row keeps the object id as `principal` and its `principalType`, carries no
  `principalStatus`, and is named unread as `roleAssignments/<role> -> <principal id> @ <scope>/principal`
  with the cause `Could not look up the principal of a role assignment through directoryObjects/getByIds: ...`.
- **Found.** The name: a user by its user principal name, a group by the rule of
  [#roster-identity-and-shared-names](#roster-identity-and-shared-names), a service principal by its
  display name. A principal the directory returns as another type, a device for one, is written by its
  object id, as it was before the lookup searched every type (a deviation from the letter of R-3 that
  Task 2 raised and the review kept):
  `principalType` cannot name it, and its display name alone would be applied as a group of that name,
  a wrong-write path.
- **Not found.** The object id, with `principalStatus` from the deleted items read: `Deleted` or
  `Unresolved`. When that read fails the row is `Unresolved` AND named unread as `.../principalStatus`:
  the getByIds batch succeeded without the principal, so it is certainly not a live readable object
  the engine could create an assignment for, and only the reason is unread.
- **principalType** is written for EVERY row whose Azure Resource Manager type maps to the schema enum
  (User, Group, ServicePrincipal, and ForeignGroup as Group), and left out for any other type. The key
  order is `scope, role, principal, principalType, principalStatus, description, condition,
  conditionVersion, id`, each where present.
- **The order of the splits.** The root scope first (a root row stays in the root list only), then the
  scope no document can declare ([#undeclarable-scope](#undeclarable-scope)), then the collision pass,
  then the status step, so the role and principal it names are the ones written.

One warning per call counts the rows with `principalStatus`, and one information record tagged
`Omnicit.EntraRBAC.UnresolvedPrincipal` (type `Omnicit.EntraRBAC.UnresolvedPrincipalNotice`) hands over
the warning and the rows: `RoleAssignmentId`, `Scope`, `Role`, `Principal`, `PrincipalType`,
`PrincipalStatus` and `StatusRead` (fix round 1, F1: false where the deleted items read failed, so a
reader never states the reason of such an `Unresolved` as a fact; a row without the member is read the
same way). Standalone, the unread entries join the call's own `InventoryPartial`. Under an export,
which calls each scope with `-ErrorAction Stop`, where that error would skip the whole scope, they go
to the run context instead ([#export-run-context](#export-run-context)), and the export names them in
`IncompleteReads`, after the Entra ID entries and before the role policy selection entries, and in a
clause of its own in its `InventoryPartial`. The export suppresses the per-scope warnings, deduplicates
the rows on the role assignment id (on scope, role and principal for a row with none) without regard
to letter case, warns once before its `ShouldProcess`, and hands the rows to the README section "Role
assignments whose principal the directory did not return". Cost if wrong: a finding the operator
reviews; the assignment stays in the document either way.

**A failed Azure read is an unread section (Sprint 11 step 10, BL-34, BL-155 first point, R-3).** No
single anchor explains the inventory's unread sections, and this one already says how a failed
`roleAssignments` read reaches `InventoryPartial`, so the rule for the two Azure sections is written here.
`Get-OERRoleAssignment` and `Get-OERRoleManagementPolicy` publish a failure as a non-terminating record
(`InvalidScope`, `AmbiguousFilter`, `RoleDefinitionNotFound`, `PolicyNotFound`, `RoleEnumerationFailed` or
the ARM read's own), and `Get-OERInventory` used to read them as they came: a standalone call wrote the
section empty, or with the part that was read, left the record on the caller's stream and named nothing in
`InventoryPartial`, a failed read stated as an empty fact (G3). Now each read runs with `-ErrorAction Stop`
inside a `try`. The `catch` scrubs the record first (`Remove-OERErrorRecord`) and calls `Add-UnreadSection`
with the key `roleAssignments` or `roleManagementPolicies` and the cause `Could not read role assignments:`
or `Could not read role management policies:` followed by the reader's own message, trimmed of trailing white
space and then of trailing full stops (the controller's ruling R-18, in fix round 1; the first commit left
the message as it was, and a message that ends in a period showed two in the clause). The clause adds its
own full stop, and the lookups the readers call (`Resolve-OERRoleDefinitionId`,
`Get-OERRoleManagementPolicyId`) throw messages that end in one, so the common `-Role` failure
(`RoleDefinitionNotFound`, `PolicyNotFound`) would otherwise end `..`. The Undecided cause of the same
function is trimmed the same way. The section is written
empty, and the code after the read finds nothing to do for it: no principal lookup, and no root scope or
undeclarable scope notice for the call. The section is read whole or not at all. An assignment inside the
`try` gets none of what the reader wrote before it failed, and the policy section stands in ONE `try`
around every `Get-OERRoleManagementPolicy` call, so with `-Role A,B` where B fails the policy of A is not
written either: a section is never a subset presented as the whole. The first failure ends the read, so
the roles after B are not read. The record is folded into the cause and not republished, and no warning
is written: `InventoryPartial`, after the inventory object, is the report (the catalog list's form).
`-CommonRoles` is the exception, and the reader is not changed in this step (R-19, fix round 1; the first
commit's text said the reader skips "a curated role that does not exist in the subscription", which is
less than it does). `Get-OERRoleManagementPolicy -CommonRoles` reads each curated role on its own and, in
its per-role `catch`, skips ANY role whose definition or policy it cannot read -- a refused or failed ARM
read, an ambiguous name or no policy as much as a role missing at the scope -- with its own warning
(`Skipping role '<name>': <message>`), and carries on. The section then holds the policies of the roles
that were read, which may be fewer than the curated set, and it is not reported partial: a refused read
stated as an absent role is the failed-read-as-a-fact gap this section closes everywhere else, left open
here because the reader is outside this step, and raised as a finding. Only a scope the reader cannot
resolve (`InvalidScope`), or a sign-in or Azure Resource Manager token its own `begin` cannot get
(`ArmTokenAcquisitionFailed`, which the inherited `Stop` makes terminating, or the terminating
`SignInRefused` when this command's own sign-in left it latched), reaches `Get-OERInventory`'s `catch`
under `-CommonRoles`; the test fixtures write `InvalidScope` for that call, and the `-CommonRoles` per-role
failures are driven through the REAL reader
with its helpers mocked (a mock of the reader cannot show them). Under a Stop warning preference
(`-WarningAction Stop`, or a global `$WarningPreference` set to `Stop`) the stop at that
`Skipping role` warning leaves the reader as a terminating error, which the policy section's `try` catches: the section is
named unread, with the warning's text as its cause, and the command carries on (measured, both forms; the
command used to stop at that warning). That is the safe direction, the section named and not a subset
presented as the whole, and it is stated in the help.

Under `Export-OERInventory`, whose per-scope call passes `-ErrorAction Stop`, the new `InventoryPartial`
is what makes the export skip the scope, as the reader's own record did before: the scope is named in
`SkippedScopes`, its rows are not written, and the skip's warning carries the cause. Cost if wrong: an
operator who wants the reader's own record rather than the cause sees it only inside `InventoryPartial`;
the `catch` can republish it after the bookkeeping, and a warning can be added there too.

**Measured, with the tests.** The engine puts the reader's record into a caller's `-ErrorVariable` the
instant the reader writes it, before any `catch` runs ([#writeerror-deposit](#writeerror-deposit)). A
standalone call with `-ErrorVariable` on a failed `roleAssignments` read collected that record twice,
beside `InventoryPartial`, and `$global:Error` held only `InventoryPartial`, since `Remove-OERErrorRecord`
had removed the reader's. The error STREAM carries only `InventoryPartial`, which is what the tests read
(`2>&1`). The record's bearer token is scrubbed in every copy. Fix round 1 pinned both halves in the
no-`try` runspace test of a failed `roleAssignments` read (R-17): the runspace's `$Error` holds only
`InventoryPartial` after the call, and with the error stream merged into the output the inventory object
comes first and `InventoryPartial` after it. A throw the REAL `-CommonRoles` reader catches for itself
reaches a caller's `-ErrorVariable` as well (13 records for one skipped role, measured with the reader's
helpers mocked, which may count each mock frame), so that path's tests read the error stream and not the
variable. A Pester mock runs under the test's own
`Stop` preference, so it cannot tell a call with `-ErrorAction Stop` from one without: the proof that each
of the four reads (the assignments and the three policy branches) carries the parameter is a script with no
`try` above it, in a runspace whose preference is `Continue`, where each dropped parameter turns exactly
its own test red.

**Mutation proofs (R-3).** Made in the source of the step's Task 1 commit; lines are the commit's.

| Id | Guard | Mutant | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | the assignment read's `try`, `Get-OERInventory.ps1:1628` | the original unguarded call | 4 red |
| M1b | its `-ErrorAction Stop`, `:1629` | dropped | 1 red, the no-`try` runspace test |
| M1c, M1d, M1e | the unread entry, its cause and its key, `:1633` | entry dropped; message dropped from the cause; key `roleAssignment` | 4, 4 and 3 red; the export skip test red for the first |
| M2a, M2b, M2c | `-ErrorAction Stop` on each policy branch, `:2519`, `:2520`, `:2521` | each dropped | 1 red each, the no-`try` runspace test of its branch |
| M2d | the policy read's single `try`, `:2517` | the original unguarded block | 8 red |
| M2e, M2g | the unread entry and its key, `:2526` | entry dropped; key `roleManagementPolicy` | 7 red each |
| M2f | one `try` around the whole read, `:2521` | one `try` per role | 3 red |
| E1 | the export's per-scope `-ErrorAction Stop`, `Export-OERInventory.ps1:1137` | dropped | 2 red, one per section |
| S1, S2 | the scrub first in each `catch`, `Get-OERInventory.ps1:1630`, `:2523` | scrub removed | 1 red each, the bearer-token hygiene gate of `tests/QA/sourcehygiene.tests.ps1` |

**Mutation proofs (fix round 1).** Made in the source and tests of the fix round's commit; lines are those of
the files before this paragraph was written.

| Id | Guard | Mutant | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | the stand-in's id in `tests/Unit/Private/Get-OERScopeSpellingProblem.Tests.ps1:225` | `SubscriptionId = $null` | 1 red, the test that has `Get-OERInventory` leave a role assignment out exactly when the owner returns a problem |
| F2a, F2b | the trim of the assignment cause, `Get-OERInventory.ps1:1646`, and of the policy cause, `:2547` | no trim | 3 and 9 red, the R-18 tests (three endings, and three policy branches) |
| F2c, F2d | the white space trim of each cause, same lines | full stops only | 1 and 3 red, the ending with white space after the period |
| F4 | a `-Subscription` verdict decided on the holder, `:808` | the verdict's own id | 1 red, the `NoSubscription` answer with an id |
| F5 | the scrub in the assignment `catch`, `:1641` | removed | 1 red, the R-17 runspace test, besides the static gate (S1) |
| F3 | the policy read's `try`, `:2537` | the original unguarded block | 2 red, the Stop warning preference tests of the real `-CommonRoles` reader |
| F6 | the assignment read's `try`, `:1638` | the original unguarded call | 1 red, the first assignment test (it stops at the call: the reader's record is terminating under the test's `Stop`) |

**R-4 (the apply engine; A18).** `Sync-OERStructureRoleAssignment` takes the `principal` of an entry
that declares `principalStatus` as the object id it names, with no principal lookup at all, for the
entry and for it as a sibling in the key rows; one whose principal is not an object id is `Failed` with
no lookup and no error record, which only a caller that skips the validator can reach. The root scope
check stays first. The role lookup, the duplicate check and the read at the scope run as for any entry,
so a matching live assignment is `Unchanged`, or `Updated` on declared drift, and one inherited from an
ancestor scope is `Skipped` as before. Where the entry would CREATE the assignment it is `Skipped`, with
the Detail `principalStatus '<value>': the principal '<principal>' could not be looked up when the
document was exported, so the apply engine never creates a role assignment for this entry. Nothing was
written. Remove the entry, or name a principal that exists and remove principalStatus`, with no
`ShouldProcess` and no `New-OERRoleAssignment`, so a plan and a real run report the same row. The prune
pass is unchanged: the entry's key is its object id and the role, so it protects the live assignment,
and a document without the entry lets `-Prune` remove it like any undeclared assignment at a declared
scope. The ruling: the specification's "before every lookup" is read as "before any principal lookup
and before any create path", since the role lookup and the read at the scope are what make the
`Unchanged` row and the prune protection possible. Cost if wrong: a create the document's author
wanted is never sent until the entry names a principal that exists.

**R-5 (the validator and the schema).** `principalStatus` is a known key of `roleAssignments` only (an
unknown key, a Warning, in `directoryRoleAssignments`) and an enum of `Resolve-OERStructureEnumCasing`
(`Deleted`, `Unresolved`): any other value, or a value that is not a string, is an Error, and a
non-canonical letter case a Warning, which `Read-OERStructureDocument` canonicalises before the engine
reads it. A declared `principalStatus` requires `principal` to be an object id (`Test-OERGuid`), or the
`principal` is an Error. An explicit null is not declared. The schema declares the enum and a
description that tells a model what the engine does and never to add the key itself.

**The scope of BL-133 here (ruling).** The Azure `roleAssignments` section only. Directory role
assignments, group eligibility, reviewers and catalog resources keep `Resolve-OERPrincipalName`'s
default path: a principal they cannot name is written by its object id, with no status and no deleted
items read, and a failed lookup there is still not told apart from a principal that is gone. A known
limit, raised as a finding.

**Known limits.** (a) The scope above. (b) An assignment several scopes read can be looked up
differently by each, and the export merges the scopes' rows on scope, role and principal (no id
without `-IncludeId`). Where one scope's getByIds batch fails and another's succeeds without the
principal, both rows carry the object id and so share a key; the merge keeps each key's index, and a
row with `principalStatus` takes the place of a kept row without it, so the assignment is written once
with its status whichever scope read it first. Its `.../principal` entry, and the cause beside it, is
then left out of `IncompleteReads` and the `InventoryPartial` clause, since another scope read the
principal (the whole-branch review of Sprint 11 step 6 found the first-row-wins merge writing the row
without a status, while the warning and the README named it `Deleted` or `Unresolved`, and the
never-create guard was lost for it). What remains: where one scope's batch fails and another's FINDS
the principal, one row is written by object id and one by name, so the keys differ and the
assignment is written twice, and the failed lookup stays unread. Applying that is not destructive:
the engine resolves both to one key, reports the later entry `Failed` as a repeat, and keeps its key
declared ([#role-assignment-key](#role-assignment-key)). (c) The `roleAssignments`
section no longer shares the principal name cache of the other sections, so a principal named in both
`roleAssignments` and `directoryRoleAssignments` costs two lookups per call. (d) A root-scope row's
principal is looked up like any other, which is how the root list names it, but it is not looked for
among the deleted items, and a failed lookup of it is not reported. (e) A scope the export skips after
its per-scope call -- its role management policy list fails, say -- merges none of its rows, so the
export takes back what that call handed over: its rows with `principalStatus`, its rows at a scope no
document can declare ([#undeclarable-scope](#undeclarable-scope)), and its unread principal entries
with their causes, each list to the count it had before the scope. The warnings, the README and
`IncompleteReads` therefore name no row that only a skipped scope read, and the skipped scope itself is
what the bundle reports for it. Two things still outlive the skip: the root notices, since a root row
is left out of the document whichever scope read it and the warning says just that, and the answers
of the deleted items read that the call kept in the run context, which are facts read and not rows.

### CLAUDE.md text for unresolved-principals

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Get-OERDeletedPrincipalStatus` is the single read of `directory/deletedItems`, and
  `Resolve-OERPrincipalName -Detailed` the lookup that tells a principal the directory returned from
  one it did not return and from one whose lookup failed** (BL-133, A18). Only the `roleAssignments`
  section of `Get-OERInventory` uses both. `-Detailed` alone has two more callers since Sprint 11
  step 8, neither of which reads the deleted items: the `administrativeUnits` section's scoped role
  type lookup, and `Get-OERServicePrincipalAccess` for the users named in delegated permission
  grants (see the next bullet). In the `roleAssignments` section a principal not returned is written
  by its object id with `principalStatus` `Deleted` or `Unresolved`, and a failed lookup or a failed
  deleted items read is
  never a fact -- it is named unread (`.../principal`, `.../principalStatus`; the second still written
  `Unresolved`, never as a principal that exists). The read never throws, never writes an error
  record, and caches only an answer that was read. `Sync-OERStructureRoleAssignment` looks no principal
  up for an entry that declares `principalStatus` and never creates its assignment (`Skipped`, no
  `ShouldProcess`). The other sections keep `Resolve-OERPrincipalName`'s default map, which is
  unchanged. Never read `directory/deletedItems` anywhere else.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#unresolved-principals`

## undeclarable-scope

Sprint 11 step 6 (A13, A15; ruling R-6) gave the two scope spelling rules one owner and made the export
leave out a role assignment at a scope no document can declare. This anchor records the problem, the
rulings and the known limits. `Get-OERScopeSpellingProblem` is the single owner of the rules (CLAUDE.md,
Code Style). The measurements behind the rules themselves are in
[#role-assignment-key](#role-assignment-key); nothing new was measured in this step.

**The problem.** The validator refuses, as an Error, a `roleAssignments` or `roleManagementPolicies`
scope with a trailing or doubled `/` (A15) and a path scope with a `.` or `..` segment, a `%`, a `\`, a
`?` or a `#`, or white space it refuses (A13). The names of a few Azure resource types can hold such a
character, and `Get-OERInventory` reads role assignments at a subscription or a management group
without `atScope()`, so an assignment at such a resource below it was exported with its scope as Azure
Resource Manager returns it. The validator then refused the whole exported document, and the operator
had to find and remove the entry by hand.

**R-6 (one owner).** `Get-OERScopeSpellingProblem -Scope -Path` holds both rules, moved from the
validator verbatim, and returns one `Rule` and `Message` per broken rule, in the order the validator
reports them (`Slash`, then `DotSegment`, `Escape`, `Backslash`, `QueryOrFragment` and `WhiteSpace`),
with the validator's exact message for the path given; the `mg:`, `sub:` and `subscription:` forms are
exempt from the segment rules, decided by `ConvertTo-OERScopeSplat`. It is pure. The validator's two
functions add one Error per problem and decide no spelling themselves: every validator test passed
unchanged, which is the refactor's proof, and an agreement test holds the validator, the owner and the
export's filter to one answer over seventeen scopes. Its help is the reference list of the rules (Task
7 of this step, and its fix round, took the copies out of the help of `Test-OERStructureSchema`,
`Get-OERStructureSchemaJson`, `Get-OERInventory` and `Export-OERInventory`, the validator's source
comments and the bundle README, which now point at a list or give an example). Five texts still list
the rules for their readers, and a new rule must reach each: README.md, the about topic, the two scope
descriptions in the schema JSON (the list a model validates against), the CLAUDE.md bullet of
`ConvertTo-OERCanonicalScope`, and `Get-OERInventory`'s words for each rule in the Reason; no gate
holds them, so the owner's help names them. Cost if wrong: two copies of a rule that only a test
keeps in step.

**The export leaves the row out.** `Get-OERInventory` calls the owner on each projected role
assignment's scope after the root split and before the collision pass and the principal status step:
a root row stays in the root list only; an undeclarable row never changes how another row is named;
its principal is never looked for among the deleted items, and a failed lookup of it is never reported.
One warning per call counts the rows, and one information record tagged
`Omnicit.EntraRBAC.UndeclarableScope` (type `Omnicit.EntraRBAC.UndeclarableScopeNotice`) hands over the
warning and the rows: `RoleAssignmentId`, `Scope`, `Role`, `Principal`, `PrincipalType` and `Reason`,
which names the broken rules in words that hold no character the README's Markdown reads as markup.
`Export-OERInventory` suppresses the per-scope warnings, deduplicates the rows on the role assignment
id (on scope, role and principal for a row with none) without regard to letter case, warns once
before its `ShouldProcess`, and lists them in the README section "Role assignments at a scope
no document can declare". The row is left out, not unread: it is not named in `IncompleteReads` and
raises no `InventoryPartial`. Cost if wrong: an assignment the operator wanted in the document is only
in the README, and a document carrying it is refused anyway.

**It is never pruned.** The engine prunes only an assignment DEFINED at a scope a document declares
(the handler compares the live assignment's scope with the declared one exactly), and no document can
declare such a scope, so such an assignment is never a prune candidate, and leaving it out of the
document removes nothing.

**Known limits.** (a) Role management policies at such a scope are NOT filtered. The walk lists
management groups and subscriptions only, so such a policy is reachable only through a `-Scope` the
operator gives `Get-OERInventory` or `Export-OERInventory`; a document that then carries it is refused
by the validator as before. (b) The words of each rule live in `Get-OERInventory` beside the record, not
in the owner, whose shape R-6 fixed at `Rule` and `Message`: a rule added to the owner without words is
named by its `Rule` name, never left out of the reason. (c) The directory role sections are not
affected: their `/` is the Microsoft Entra tenant scope.

#### CLAUDE.md text for undeclarable-scope (step 11c)

Moved from CLAUDE.md in step 11c (BL-160, A26): the mechanics; the rule stays in CLAUDE.md.

The text stands in full under the older CLAUDE.md copy at
[#role-assignment-key](#role-assignment-key) (its heading "CLAUDE.md text for role-assignment-key"),
which holds the `Get-OERScopeSpellingProblem` bullet as CLAUDE.md worded it before this step. What
moved out of the bullet, in short: the validator's two functions, `Add-ScopeSlashFinding` and
`Add-ScopeSegmentFinding`, add one Error per problem the owner returns and decide no spelling;
`Get-OERInventory` writes one warning and one `Omnicit.EntraRBAC.UndeclarableScope` record per call;
`Get-OERSubscriptionHomeTenant` resolves and reads nothing for a raw scope it rates `Undecided`, so an
`Export-OERInventory -Scope` spelled so is unread (the paragraph "The export leaves the row out"
above holds the rest).

## restricted-unit-pim

Sprint 11 step 6 (BL-134, ruling R-7) made the export name, and the validator warn about, a group that
uses PIM for Groups and is a member of a restricted management administrative unit. This anchor records
what Microsoft documents, what is not measured, the rulings and the known limits. No request was added.

**What Microsoft Learn states (as fact).** The PIM for Groups articles ("Bring groups into Privileged
Identity Management", "Assign eligibility for a group in Privileged Identity Management", "Configure
PIM for Groups settings") each say: "Privileged Identity Management doesn't support groups in
Restricted Management Administrative Units (RMAU)." And "Restricted management administrative units in
Microsoft Entra ID", under Limitations, item 2: "Groups and users in a restricted management
administrative unit can't be managed with Microsoft Entra ID Governance features such as Privileged
Identity Management, Entitlement management, Lifecycle workflows and Access reviews." The texts state
the limit as fact and name its source; an earlier wording that only said a tenant-level identity "may
not be able to" manage such a group was withdrawn on review, since it suggested an identity scoped to
the unit could.

**What is not measured.** What Microsoft Graph answers when the apply engine sends a PIM eligibility or
a PIM for Groups policy write for such a group. So every text says that `Invoke-OERStructure` still
sends those writes, and nothing claims a particular answer. A live checklist item that measures it
would close BL-134.

**R-7 (the export).** With `Groups` and `AdministrativeUnits` both included, `Export-OERInventory`
checks, before it strips the object ids, each group `inventory.json` keeps that carries a `pimPolicy`
(a present key that is not null) or an eligibility with at least one entry, against every
administrative unit whose `restricted` is the boolean true and whose `members` were read: a unit that
lists the group's object id, compared without regard to letter case, makes one entry of the group and
its units. One warning before the bundle's `ShouldProcess` counts the groups, and the README section
"Groups using PIM for Groups in a restricted management unit" names each group and its units by display
name, never by id. Nothing is left out of the export. A unit whose `members` are an explicit null
(unread, and named in `IncompleteReads`) lists nobody. A dynamic unit carries no `members`, which is no
gap: Microsoft Learn states that administrative units with rules for dynamic membership groups for
groups are not supported, so a group is never a member of one. Without either section there are no
groups or no units, so nothing is found and nothing is read for it. Cost if wrong: a finding the
operator reviews.

**The validator (Rule 16).** A Warning, never an Error: an Error would refuse a document that may well
apply, while the limit is documented and the answer unmeasured. A group that uses PIM for Groups -- a
`pimPolicy` that is not null, or an `eligibility` array with at least one entry -- draws it at
`groups[i].administrativeUnit` when that reference names a restricted `administrativeUnits[]` entry,
read as Rule 12 reads it (an object id, parsed with `-as [guid]`, matches the entry that declares that
id; any other value matches by display name, ignoring case; one local helper serves both rules), and at
`groups[i]` when such a unit's `members` list the group by its name (a template's computed name
included) or its declared id, ignoring case; each shape at most once per unit. An exported document
raises neither shape: its groups carry no object id and no `administrativeUnit`, and its units list a
group member by object id, which the document declares nowhere. The shapes fire on a hand-written
document and on `Get-OERInventory -IncludeId` output, which carries the ids.

**Known limits.** (a) The Graph answer is not measured (above). (b) A restricted unit left out of the
document because another unit shares its name is not in what `Get-OERInventory` returns, so it is not
checked; it is named as a shared name and in `IncompleteReads`. (c) `Get-OERInventory` on its own does
not check: it carries no group ids without `-IncludeId`. A finding, if a later step wants it. (d) The
validator cannot see the export's case (above), which is why the export warns on its own.

### CLAUDE.md text for restricted-unit-pim

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **A group that uses PIM for Groups in a restricted management administrative unit is a Warning,
  never an Error or a refusal**: `Export-OERInventory` warns before its `ShouldProcess` (with `Groups`
  and `AdministrativeUnits` included, from what it read, with no request) and lists the groups in the
  bundle README, and validator Rule 16 warns on a document that places such a group in a restricted
  unit it declares. State the limit as Microsoft Learn documents it, as fact, and what Microsoft Graph
  answers to the engine's PIM writes for such a group as unmeasured until a live run measures it.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#restricted-unit-pim`

## review-package-in-the-same-run

Sprint 11 step 6 (BL-147, ruling R-8) put every `accessPackages` entry's package into the run's rename
map, so an access review reaches the package its own document's entry found or created, and never one
of that name in another catalog. This anchor records the problem, the rulings, the residual R-8 accepts
and the known limits. `Resolve-OERStructureRename` stays the single owner of the map's keys. No ErrorId
and no public parameter was added. The rules were derived from the code and proven with mocked tests;
nothing here was measured live.

**The problem (BL-147).** The map held only a package the document renames
([#rename-policies-and-reviews](#rename-policies-and-reviews)). A review that named by display name a
package the document declares without a rename was resolved like any name, in the whole tenant: by the
target check (`Resolve-OERAccessPackageId`) and by the create (`Resolve-OERAccessReviewScopeTarget`).
So for a package declared in catalog A while a package of that name exists in catalog B, the review was
checked against, or created on, B's package -- the mocked test for it showed the create looking the
name up and finding B's package. Step 5's guard already failed the package itself when
`New-OERAccessPackage` returned another catalog's ([#roster-identity-and-shared-names](#roster-identity-and-shared-names),
known limit (c)); the review was the remaining path.

**R-8 (every entry in the map).** `Resolve-OERStructureRename` gains two parameter sets for an
`accessPackages` entry that renames nothing: `-Identified -Id` registers `accesspackages|<name>` with the
package's id, and `-Unidentified -Reason` registers it refused, with no id and no ErrorId. Both carry no
previous name (`PreviousName` null), which is how a reader tells such an entry from a rename's; any
other section, or `-Identified` without an id, is a caller error thrown before anything is registered.
`Sync-OERStructureAccessPackage` marks every entry with a non-empty `displayName` and no
`previousDisplayName` refused first ("the accessPackages entry did not find or create it; see that
entry's rows"), and registers the package's id as soon as it has the package: the existing package
found in the declared catalog, before anything else is read or written for it (also after a `Current`
rename outcome), or the package it created there, once the created package is shown not to be another
catalog's (an answer with no id leaves the refusal). A rename keeps its own registration. A stop before
that -- the catalog refused, a failed or ambiguous lookup, a refused rename, a failed create, a create
that returned another catalog's package -- leaves the refusal, and a failure after it (an update, the
resource role bindings, the policies) does not take the id back. `Invoke-OERStructure`, when `-Include`
leaves out AccessPackages, registers every entry that renames nothing refused, with the reason "the
accessPackages section is not selected by -Include".

**The review reads it.** `Sync-OERStructureAccessReview` reads the map for a package NAME (an object id
is never a key). A registered id replaces the name in the copy the target check and the create read, so
neither looks the name up, and the policy is resolved within the package by that id; a `Failed` row of
the target check says "accessPackage '...' was read as '...', the access package its accessPackages
entry resolved in this run". A refusal is one `Failed` row, "access package '...' has no id in this run
(reason), so the access package this access review reviews cannot be identified; nothing was created,
read or written for it", with no error record and nothing read: it does not speak of a rename. Cost if
wrong: a review the operator expected to apply is refused, and never written to the wrong package.

**Rule 15, widened.** Every entry now registers its package under the name key, so two entries of one
display name in two catalogs would replace each other's registration whether or not one renames. The
validator therefore refuses, as an Error, a review that names by display name a package two or more
`accessPackages` entries declare (as `displayName` or as a `previousDisplayName` that renames), with or
without a rename; its message names the rename only when one of the entries renames, so the rename-case
texts are unchanged. Cost: such a document, which applied before when no entry renamed, must now name
the review's package by its object id.

**The residual R-8 accepts (`-WhatIf`).** A package the plan would create has no id yet, so it is
registered refused ("the accessPackages entry would create it, and the create was not carried out:
-WhatIf, or a declined confirmation"), and the plan reports the review `Failed` while a real run creates
the package first and then the review. A declined confirmation of the package's create gives the same
refusal. Accepted: the plan errs towards refusing, never towards a review on another package.

**The `-Include` refusal.** With `-Include` leaving out AccessPackages, nothing is read for the
package entries, so the run cannot know which package a declared name means: every review that names a
declared package by display name is refused, renamed or not, with no error record, so `-ErrorAction
Stop` and `$?` do not see it. A review that names the package by object id, or a package the document
does not declare, is resolved as before. Cost: a run that selects `AccessReviews` without
`AccessPackages` refuses reviews it applied before; include `AccessPackages`, or name the package by
its object id.

**Known limits.** (a) The `-Include` marks of the assignment policies under the package's name are no
longer reached by a review that names the package by name, since the package's refusal is read first;
they are kept, and matter again only if that order or that key ever changes. (b) The `-WhatIf` residual
above. (c) Rule 15 refuses offline a document it accepted before (two same-named packages in two
catalogs and a review naming that name). The release note does not list it (the controller's ruling on
Task 7's review): only a hand-written document reaches it. An export can write two `accessPackages`
entries of one name, one per catalog ([#roster-identity-and-shared-names](#roster-identity-and-shared-names),
R-5), but it names a review's access package by its object id whenever another package in the tenant
carries that name ([#access-review-target](#access-review-target), since Sprint 11 step 5), and Rule
15 never reads a reference that is an object id. The refusal names the entries and says to name the
package by its object id.

### CLAUDE.md text for review-package-in-the-same-run

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Resolve-OERStructureRename` is the single owner of the keys of the run's rename map, and every
  `accessPackages` entry registers its package there, not only a rename** (BL-147): an entry that
  renames nothing through `-Identified -Id` once it has found the package in its catalog or created it
  there, and through `-Unidentified -Reason` (refused, no ErrorId) until then; such an entry carries
  no previous name, which is how a reader tells it from a rename and words its rows. So
  `Sync-OERStructureAccessReview` reads a declared package's name only through the map and never
  looks it up in the whole tenant; with `-Include` leaving AccessPackages out every such review is
  refused. Validator Rule 15 refuses a review that names by display name a package two or more
  `accessPackages` entries declare, with or without a rename. Never register a map key outside the
  owner, and never let a review resolve a declared package's name past a refusal.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#review-package-in-the-same-run`

## naming-standard

Sprint 11 step 7 (A6, A9) made the naming standard data. `Test-OERStructure -NamingStandard` reads a JSON
file and adds one Warning for each rule a name breaks (a segment rule once for each segment that breaks
it) to the validation of a document or of an exported `inventory.json`; `Invoke-OERStructure` never receives one, so applying a document is unchanged. The
only new public parameter is `-NamingStandard` and the only new ErrorId is `InvalidNamingStandard`.
Four functions own the pieces (CLAUDE.md, Code Style): `Test-OERNamingStandardName` the rules, their
order and their Detail texts, `Read-OERNamingStandard` reading and refusing the file,
`Get-OERNamingStandardSchemaJson` its schema, and `Test-OERStructureSchema` (Rule 17) the findings. No
request is sent: the check is offline. This anchor records the rulings behind that design and the
known limits.

**The reader checks the file by hand, and the schema is held in step.** The schema is draft-07 and is
published at `docs/examples/naming-standard.schema.json`, for an editor or an LLM. The reader does not
call `Test-Json` at run time. It checks the file against the rules the schema declares, in its own
code, for two reasons. The module's own message text is ASCII (a value the reader quotes is shown as
found, so a non-ASCII value in the file appears in it) and names every problem in one throw (a path such
as `segments[1].case`, what was expected, what was found), where a library's messages are not ours and
change with the PowerShell version's JSON Schema library. And two rules draft-07 cannot express need
the reader anyway: every `pattern` and every `exceptions` entry must compile as a .NET regular
expression, and no `values` entry may contain the separator (it could never match a segment, since a
name is split at the separator first). Matching of keys and enum values is exact (ordinal), as
draft-07 specifies, so a key or value that carries a hidden character is refused. The two cannot drift
unseen: `tests/Unit/Private/Read-OERNamingStandard.Tests.ps1`, Context "agreement with the schema",
runs every refusal case through `Test-Json -Schema` and holds that the schema refuses it too, except
the cases of those two rules, where the schema accepts and only the reader refuses; it is skipped where
`Test-Json` has no `-Schema`. `tests/Unit/Private/Get-OERNamingStandardSchemaJson.Tests.ps1`
holds the published file identical to the function's output (after LF normalization and trimming the
end) and the example standard accepted by both the reader and the published schema. The file carries
`"version": "1.0"`, an exact enum, so a later format is refused by its version and never misread.
Cost if wrong: the reader and the schema can disagree where no refusal case reaches.

**Every pattern matches the whole text; values compare ordinally.** A segment `pattern` and an
`exceptions` entry are compiled as `\A(?:pattern)\z` with `RegexOptions.CultureInvariant`, and they
are case-sensitive unless they carry `(?i)`. `-match` semantics, which find the text anywhere, would
make `Fin` accept the segment `Finance` and the exception `All Users` exempt `All Users Copy`; a closed
standard needs the whole-text reading, and an exception never exempts more than its text says. The
cost is that an operator who expects `-match` must write `Fin.*` for a prefix. A `values` entry is
compared exactly and is never read as a pattern, so `C++` and `A.B` mean what they say, and a hidden
character is a difference. Held by `Read-OERNamingStandard.Tests.ps1`
("compiles a pattern and an exception as a whole-text match") and by
`tests/Unit/Private/Test-OERNamingStandardName.Tests.ps1` (Contexts "the pattern", "the exceptions",
"the allowed values" and "a name that holds characters a pattern would read specially").
Letter cases are Unicode categories (`\p{Lu}`, `\p{Ll}`, `\p{L}`, `\p{Nd}`), so an A with a ring above
is a letter. Cost if wrong: a name an operator thought exempt is checked, or the reverse.

**An optional segment is present when the part count requires it, otherwise when the part fits.** With
R required segments, T segments and n parts, exactly n minus R optional segments are present. An
optional segment is skipped when none is left to place, takes the next part when as many optional
segments remain (from it to the end) as are still to be placed, and otherwise takes the part when it
fits the segment (one of its values or its pattern, and its letter case) and is skipped when it does
not. The count decides first, since a name with that many parts must carry that many optional segments;
the fit decides only where the count leaves a choice. Cost if wrong: a part is read as belonging to
another optional segment than the author meant, and is reported against that one. Held by "optional
segments" in `Test-OERNamingStandardName.Tests.ps1`.

**A structural rule stops the segment checks of that name.** A name with an empty segment, with no
separator where one is needed (`separator`) or with too few or too many segments (`segmentCount`) has no
reliable segment alignment, so reporting each segment's value and case against a guess would add noise
to the one finding that matters. The finding stops that name's checks; `maxLength` does not stop them,
since the length says nothing about the segments. Held by "the separator" and "the segment count" in
`Test-OERNamingStandardName.Tests.ps1` ("stops at the count and checks no segment").

**A synchronized group the standard does not include gets one Warning, decided before the exceptions
are read.** The apply engine writes nothing to a group synchronized from on-premises, so a naming
Warning on it would ask for a change that only the on-premises directory can make. By default such a
group is skipped, and its single Warning says it was not checked and how to include it
(`includeSyncedGroups`), whether or not its name would have followed the standard and even when the
name matches an exception, so the row does not depend on the name. Three shapes get another row, or
none: a synced group named by a template whose name cannot be computed gets the template row below
instead; a group that declares a `displayName` which is not a non-empty string gets no naming row (its
`template`, if any, is not read either); and a group with no `displayName` and no `template` that is a
non-empty string gets none, since the validator's own findings stand for each of those. When the
standard includes synced groups, the group is checked like any other and each finding says that its
name can only change in the on-premises directory. The check is offline, so it reads the document's own
`onPremisesSynced` key (only the boolean true counts); the apply engine decides on the live read, as
[#synced-groups](#synced-groups) records. Held by Context "a group synchronized from on-premises" in
`tests/Unit/Private/Test-OERStructureSchema.Tests.ps1`.

**A template whose name cannot be computed gets a Warning saying it was not checked.** A group declared
with `template` and `tokens` is checked on the name `Resolve-OERName` gives, at the template's path.
The name cannot be computed when a placeholder has no token, when `Resolve-OERName` refuses the result
(longer than 256 characters), or when the result is empty; a token with an empty value does resolve.
There is then no name to check, so the check says exactly that, once. The validator's own findings
about the template stand, among them, since Sprint 11 step 11, the Error at `groups[i].template` for
a template that cannot be resolved ([#naming-template-one-pass](#naming-template-one-pass)). Held by Context "a group
named by a template" in `Test-OERStructureSchema.Tests.ps1`.

**The Item of a policy's finding is the policy's own name.** An assignment policy is listed in
`sections` as `assignmentPolicies`, but its finding carries the Section `accessPackages` (the
top-level section it sits in) and the policy's own `displayName` as Item, at
`accessPackages[i].assignmentPolicies[k].displayName`, so a reader finds the policy by the name that
broke the rule and the document by the path. Held by Context "every section that carries names" in
`Test-OERStructureSchema.Tests.ps1`.

**An unreadable standard is one error, and no document is read or validated.** A path that is not a
file, a file that exists but cannot be read (a lock, no read permission), malformed JSON, a key or value
the standard does not allow or a pattern that does not compile raises the non-terminating error
`InvalidNamingStandard`, once, with the reader's message. The reader reads with `-ErrorAction Stop` for
the unreadable file: `Get-Content` writes a non-terminating error and returns nothing (measured on a
file held open with `FileShare.None`), which once reached the operator as a second error and was then
reported as an empty file. After the refusal `Test-OERStructure` returns no result for any document
(piped ones included). Validating the documents without the standard would let a broken file pass for
"no naming problems". The error is non-terminating, like the unreadable structure document's, so a
script with no `try` goes on, and the standard is read once in `begin`, never per document. Held by
Context "a standard that cannot be read", "a pipeline of documents" and "a script with no try" in
`tests/Unit/Public/Test-OERStructure.Tests.ps1`, and for the unreadable file by the Its about
`Get-Content` and a file another process holds open in both that file and
`tests/Unit/Private/Read-OERNamingStandard.Tests.ps1`: a mock cannot write a non-terminating error
(Pester runs a mock body under Stop), so the `-ErrorAction Stop` is held by a parameter filter and by
the real locked file, which those Its skip where the platform does not enforce the lock.

**The same check works on an exported inventory.** The export's own `inventory.json` is the document;
`tests/Unit/Public/Export-OERInventory.Tests.ps1` ("the exported inventory.json is checked against a
naming standard") reads a bundle back through the real `Test-OERStructure`. Held end to end for the
shipped examples by `tests/Unit/Public/Test-OERStructure.Tests.ps1` (the apply example against the
example standard: still Valid, one Warning for each rule a name breaks).

**Known limits.** (a) `ConvertFrom-Json` turns a string that holds an ISO 8601 date and time into a
`DateTime`, so such a string anywhere in the naming standard file is refused as not a string. Measured
on PowerShell 7.6.6, with `-Depth 32 -NoEnumerate` as the reader calls it: `2024-01-01T10:00:00`,
`2024-01-01T10:00:00Z` and `2024-01-01T10:00:00.5+02:00` become a `DateTime`, while `2024-01-01`,
`2024-01-01T10:00` and `2024-01-01 10:00:00` stay a string. This is a limit of the parser, not
something the reader fixes. `Read-OERStructureDocument` parsed structure documents the same way
until Sprint 11 step 11, and now adds `-DateKind String` where `ConvertFrom-Json` has it (PowerShell
7.5 or later), so a structure document keeps its text there
([#structure-document-text](#structure-document-text)); the naming standard reader does not. (b)
The check reads the document it is given. An object the export left out of `inventory.json` is not in
the document and so is not checked: a name two or more objects share, a role assignment at a scope no
document can declare (the bundle's `README.md` lists those), and a group the export does not keep. By
default `inventory.json` holds the RBAC-relevant security groups only (a role-assignable group, one
with PIM eligibility, one with a `pimPolicy`); `Export-OERInventory -AllGroupsDetailed` keeps every
group `inventory.json` covers in full detail, `-IncludeSyncedGroups` keeps the synchronized ones, and
a group whose `securityEnabled` is false, a Microsoft 365 group or a distribution group, is in
`groupsRoster.json` only at every detail level, as is every other group the export did not keep. So
the standard's `includeSyncedGroups` changes an export's findings only when the export was made with
`Export-OERInventory -IncludeSyncedGroups` (or `-AllGroupsDetailed`), a different switch with a
similar name. (c) The standard does not model Microsoft Graph's own limits on a display name: it is
advisory, and a name that follows it can still be refused when it is applied, as one that breaks it can
be accepted. (d) Of the conflicts between a `values` entry and the rest of the standard, the reader
refuses two: a segment that declares both `values` and `pattern`, and a value that contains the
separator. A value that breaks its own segment's `case` (for
example `sg` under `UPPERCASE`) is accepted, and a name that carries it gets the `values` or the `case`
Warning, so the output shows it. (e) Patterns are compiled without a match timeout, so a pattern with
catastrophic backtracking (such as `(a+)+b`) can make the offline check slow on a long name (measured:
about 1.5 s at 24 characters, growing exponentially). The check is offline and sends nothing.

### CLAUDE.md text for naming-standard

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

The rules a name must follow are a separate matter, held in a naming standard file that
`Test-OERStructure -NamingStandard` checks offline; `Test-OERNamingStandardName` owns them (see **Code
Style**). `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#naming-standard`

- **`Test-OERNamingStandardName` is the single owner of the naming rules, their order and their Detail
  texts; `Read-OERNamingStandard` of reading and refusing the naming standard file; and
  `Get-OERNamingStandardSchemaJson` of its schema.** `Test-OERStructureSchema` (Rule 17) adds one
  Warning per object and broken rule, only when `Test-OERStructure -NamingStandard` hands it a standard,
  and `Invoke-OERStructure` never passes one: a naming finding is never an Error, and applying a
  document is unchanged. Every pattern matches the whole text, values compare ordinally, and a file
  the reader refuses is `InvalidNamingStandard`, once, with no document read or validated. The reader
  checks the file by hand and never calls `Test-Json`; `docs/examples/naming-standard.schema.json` is
  the schema function's output, held identical by a test, and is never edited by hand. Never
  re-implement a rule, a Detail text or the file's validation elsewhere.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#naming-standard`

## service-principal-access

Sprint 11 step 8 (decision A7; A9 allows its one new public parameter) gave the export read-only
context on the app roles and delegated permission grants of a tenant's service principals and on the
owners of its service principals and app registrations:
`Export-OERInventory -IncludeServicePrincipalAccess` writes `servicePrincipalAccess.json`. A service
principal's Microsoft Entra directory roles and Azure roles are not in that file but in
`directoryRoleAssignments.json` and `roleAssignments.json`, each within its own coverage, so a
service principal the file does not name is not shown to be without privilege (the step's final
review narrowed every text that said the file held what service principals "may do"). This anchor
records the measurement and the ruling that chose the read's shape, the shapes and their limits, the
rulings with what each costs if it is wrong, and the mutation proofs. `Get-OERServicePrincipalAccess`
is the single reader and `ConvertTo-OERPrincipalType` the single owner of the Graph type mapping
(CLAUDE.md, Code Style). The switch is the only new public parameter; no ErrorId and no property of
the export's output object was added (Ruling R-3: `Files` names the file and `IncompleteReads` its
unread parts).

**The measurement (2026-10-18, live, reads only, as `oer-live-cc`, with the reads' own URIs, not
through the module).** No tenant value is recorded here. The test tenant held 1,129 service principals
(12 list pages with `$top=999` and a `$select` that includes `appRoles`), 175 of them with app roles,
67 app registrations (1 page), 156 delegated permission grants (1 page; `$top=999` accepted) naming 4
distinct users, 133 application permissions held by service principals (read per client), 37 app
registration owners (30 service principals and 7 users) and 1 service principal owner.

| Form | Calls in the test tenant |
|---|---|
| per client: `servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignments` for every service principal | 1,129 (+12 list) |
| per resource: `servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignedTo` for every one with app roles | 175 (+12 list), and incomplete (below) |
| expanded: `servicePrincipals?$expand=appRoleAssignments` | 12 (the list itself) |
| owners per object (`applications/{id}/owners`, `servicePrincipals/{id}/owners`) | 1,196 |
| owners expanded on the two lists | 12 + 1 |
| `oauth2PermissionGrants` | 1 |

A second round the same day: the list
`servicePrincipals?$select=id,appId,displayName,appRoles&$expand=appRoleAssignments&$top=999` takes 12
calls, keeps `appRoles` on every object, and its expanded `appRoleAssignments` (133, at most 19 per
object, none at 20) equal the per-client read for EVERY service principal, id for id. The resource side
-- `appRoleAssignedTo` per resource, or expanded on the list -- lists 131 service principal assignments,
not 133: it misses 2 that the client side shows (the resource listed, the role declared; the cause was
not measured), and 76 objects without app roles still hold `appRoleAssignedTo` rows, the default access
assignments of users and groups. An expanded app role assignment carries `appRoleId`,
`createdDateTime`, `deletedDateTime`, `id`, `principalDisplayName`, `principalId`, `principalType`,
`resourceDisplayName` and `resourceId`. The owners expanded with a nested select
(`$expand=owners($select=id,displayName,userPrincipalName)`) came back with `@odata.type`,
`displayName` and `id`, all typed and named, the same counts as the per-object reads -- so the
app-only owner reads list service principals among the owners, 30 of the 37 app registration owners.
One service principal assignment names a role its resource does not declare. `oer-live-cc` itself
holds 19 app role assignments, all on one resource, each mapped to a role value.

**Ruling R-1 (the form).** The application permissions are read from the CLIENT side, expanded on the
one service principal list the file needs anyway (12 calls there; one request per page of service
principals), with a full `servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignments?$top=999` read of any object whose
expanded list holds 20 or more: Microsoft Graph documents a maximum of 20 for an expanded directory
relationship and no next link for it, and none there reached it. The owners are read expanded on the
service principal list and on the app registration list (12 + 1), with a full `.../owners?$top=999`
read of any object with 20 or more. Since live check 1.1 (below) an object is also read in full when
one of its expanded entries lacks the id its row needs. The grants are one paged
`oauth2PermissionGrants?$top=999` list, and the users they name one `directoryObjects/getByIds` per
1,000. Measured total: 29 requests, counted in one run of the module after the re-read fix of check
1.1 (the export of `AdministrativeUnits` and `RoleAssignments` sent 35 Microsoft Graph requests with
the switch against 6 without it) -- 12 service principal list pages with their app role assignments,
2 full re-reads, 12 pages with owners, 1 app registration page, 1 grant page and 1 `getByIds` --
where the per-object reads cost about 2,340. The architect's example, one read per resource that
exposes app roles (175 calls), was rejected: measured, it is both dearer and incomplete (it misses 2
of 133). Cost if wrong: an expanded list capped below 20 for this relationship without saying so
would hide an object's permissions or owners beyond the cap; the threshold follows the documented
cap, and the measured maximum was 19.

**Measured live, check 1.1 (2026-10-18, read-only, as `oer-live-cc`), and Ruling R-14.**
`Export-OERInventory -Include AdministrativeUnits, RoleAssignments -IncludeServicePrincipalAccess`
wrote 133 application permission rows, 2 of them with `resourceId`, `resourceDisplayName` and
`appRoleValue` all `null`: rows that name no resource, and a `null` value that reads as "the resource
does not declare the role". A read-only diagnostic of those 2 measured that the expanded read
(`v1.0/servicePrincipals/{client}?$select=id&$expand=appRoleAssignments`) returns the assignment with
the `resourceId` key present and its value `null` (its keys `appRoleId`, `createdDateTime`,
`deletedDateTime`, `id`, `principalDisplayName`, `principalId`, `principalType`,
`resourceDisplayName`, `resourceId`), while the per-client read
(`v1.0/servicePrincipals/{client}/appRoleAssignments?$top=999`) returns the same assignment id with
its `resourceId` and `resourceDisplayName`; the resource exists, is named and declares the role. These
2 are also the 2 assignments the resource side never listed (R-1). So the second round's "equal ... id
for id" holds for the ids, and for these 2 the expanded values differ. A third row with
`appRoleValue` `null` is genuine: its resource (762 app roles) does not declare that role. The reader
now uses an object's expanded entries only when it holds fewer than 20 AND every entry carries the ids
its row needs -- `resourceId` and `appRoleId` for an app role assignment, `id` for an owner -- and
otherwise reads the object in full and uses that read. The owner half keeps the rule uniform: every
expanded owner measured had an id, a type and a name. **R-14:** an app role assignment that the full
read still returns without its `resourceId` or `appRoleId` leaves only `applicationPermissions`
unread -- `null`, named, with the cause "Microsoft Graph returned an app role assignment of the
service principal '...' without its resource id" (or "app role id") and the client id as its target.
The service principal list itself was read, so the grants named through it, and the owners, are
unaffected. An owner that the full read still returns without an id leaves that owners part unread.
Cost if wrong: one extra request per object whose expansion lacks an id (2 here), and, should the
full read lack the id too, a part written `null` where rows were read -- never a row that names no
resource.

**The shapes.** One JSON object, four parts in this order, each an array of rows or `null`:

- `applicationPermissions` -- one row per app role assignment a service principal holds, from the
  client side: `servicePrincipalId`, `servicePrincipalDisplayName`, `resourceId`,
  `resourceDisplayName` (the resource's name from the list, else the assignment's, else `null`),
  `appRoleId` and `appRoleValue`, the `value` of the resource's app role with that id. A default
