  access assignment (the role id `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`) carries no value, and nor
  does a role the resource no longer declares, so `appRoleValue` is `null` for both. It is also
  `null` for a role the resource declares without a value, and for a resource the service principal
  list did not return, whose name is then the assignment's own, else `null`.
- `delegatedPermissionGrants` -- one row per grant: `clientId`, `clientDisplayName`, `resourceId`,
  `resourceDisplayName` (both names from the service principal list), `consentType`, `principalId`,
  `principalDisplayName`, `principalUserPrincipalName` and `scope`, trimmed.
- `applicationOwners` and `servicePrincipalOwners` -- one row per owner, with the object's id and
  name (and an app registration's `appId`), `ownerId`, `ownerType` (`ConvertTo-OERPrincipalType` of the
  owner's `@odata.type`, else that type without its prefix, else `null`), `ownerDisplayName` and
  `ownerUserPrincipalName`.

Every id is lower-cased, every blank value is `null`, nothing is invented, and each part is sorted,
ordinally and without regard to letter case, by its display names and then its ids, so two exports of
an unchanged tenant write the same file.

**Rulings of the read.** Each with what it costs if it is wrong.

- **R-4 (without the switch, nothing).** Without the switch the reader is never called, no file is
  written, and `README.md` and `rbac-architect-prompt.md` say nothing of it: the README section, its
  `Files` bullet, the label sentence and the prompt's input bullet appear only with the switch or an
  unread entry. The step's own text changes (the prompt's `scopedRoles` keys,
  [#scoped-role-principal-type](#scoped-role-principal-type)) do change every export's prompt, so "as
  before the switch" now means "with nothing of the switch", not byte for byte the old file. Cost if
  wrong: none for consumers; slightly more code.
- **R-5 (a part is read whole or not at all).** Any failure inside a part -- its list, the full re-read
  of one object, an object listed without an id, without its `appRoles` (the roles it declares are then
  not known) or without its expanded collection (the expansion did not happen), a list answer with no
  value collection, or one user lookup that did not read -- leaves that part `null`, never `[]`, and
  names it `servicePrincipalAccess/<part>`. The grants are named through the service principal list,
  so when that list was not read they are not read at all; an app role assignment without its ids
  after the full read leaves only `applicationPermissions` unread, since the list was read (R-14).
  Cost if wrong: one failed `getByIds` batch
  hides every delegated grant of the run.
- **R-8 (both names of a grant's user).** A grant to one user carries the user's display name and its
  user principal name apart, like the owner rows; `Resolve-OERPrincipalName -Detailed` gained the two
  properties for it ([#unresolved-principals](#unresolved-principals)). Cost if wrong: one more key in
  a new file format.
- **Where it is named.** An unread part goes last in `IncompleteReads`, after the Azure Lighthouse
  entries, under a label of its own in the README, and in a clause of its own, with its causes, last in
  the export's `InventoryPartial` message. No warning is written for it. A reader that stops, or
  returns nothing, has read nothing: all four parts are then `null` and named.

**The permissions.** Microsoft Learn's tables (read 2026-10-18): "List servicePrincipals", "List
appRoleAssignments granted to a service principal", "List owners of a service principal", "List
applications" and "List owners of an application" ask for `Application.Read.All` at least, with
`Directory.Read.All` among the higher ones; "List oauth2PermissionGrants" asks for `Directory.Read.All`
at least, and `Application.Read.All` is not in its table. The export already requires
`Directory.Read.All`, so the switch needs no new permission. It is also what returns the owners'
names: Microsoft Learn states that a directory object relationship returns an object of a type the
caller cannot read with its id and type only. `tests/QA/requiredscope.tests.ps1` gained an
`applications` and an `oauth2PermissionGrants` rule (the existing `servicePrincipals` rule covers the
expanded lists and the re-reads); before them the gate accepted those literals silently, since a
literal no rule matches asks for nothing. A case there holds that the call graph carries the reader's
eight literals to `Export-OERInventory` and that each asks for exactly one rule. Measured: with
`Directory.Read.All` dropped from the export's row, the export's case names 20 unsatisfied literals,
eight of them the reader's; with the gate as it was before the two rules, 17, five of them the
reader's. The reader sends GET requests only and never names `-Method`: the gate judges every literal
of a function that sends a non-GET by its rule's write pattern.

**Known limits.** (a) The 20 cap (R-1). (b) The resource side was not used, and why it missed 2 of 133
was not measured; the client side is complete as measured. (c) The app role assignments of users and
groups -- who may sign in to an application, the 76 default access assignments among them -- are not
read: the file holds the app roles and grants service principals hold, and their directory and Azure
roles are in the two role assignment files (above). (d) An owner whose answer carries no
`userPrincipalName` is written with `ownerUserPrincipalName` `null`; the measurement recorded the keys
`@odata.type`, `displayName` and `id`. (e) The file is never applied: nothing in it is reconciled,
granted or revoked, and no validator reads it. (f) The reader was proven with mocked tests. The four
lists it reads were measured live with its URIs, and through the module by check 1.1's export. The
full read `servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignments?$top=999` was sent by check 1.1's diagnostic,
with that URI but not through the module, for the 2 clients above, and then through the module: a
run of check 1.1 on the fixed build (2026-10-18, as `oer-live-cc`), made before the gate with its
output not kept, made 2 full re-reads of app role assignments, of two different service principals,
and no owner re-read, and its export wrote 133 application permission rows with none missing an id
or a name and 1 with `appRoleValue` `null`, a role its resource (762 app roles) does not declare;
the recorded second run of check 1.1 measured the same counts. The export of `AdministrativeUnits`
and `RoleAssignments` sent 35 Microsoft Graph requests with the switch against 6 without it, so 29
for the service principal access read: the "Measured total" above is that count from one run of the
fixed module, in one tenant. Still not measured live: the re-read of an object with 20 or more
expanded entries, since no object reached 20, and the owner re-read
`.../owners?$select=id,displayName,userPrincipalName&$top=999`, never sent with that query string,
since no object's expanded owners reached 20 or lacked an id (the table above records the per-object
paths without one). A re-read Microsoft Graph refuses leaves its part unread, `null` and named, the
safe outcome. The id in a re-read's path is URI-escaped (the step's final review), which leaves a
GUID unchanged.

**Mutation proofs.** Each mutation applied to the source, the named tests run against it (a dev-mode
module, no build, for the reader; a build for the requiredscope row), the file restored and its hash
checked; the L rows (check 1.1, R-14) were applied to the built module's script, with the source line
each one names. Every mutant turned at least one test red.

| Id | Guard | Mutant | Red |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 to M4 | each part's catch sets the part `$null` | `@()` instead | the unread test of that part |
| M5 | the grants read only when the service principal list was read | `if ($true)` | the grants are read after a failed list |
| M6, M12 | a user lookup that did not read, or gave no answer, makes the grants unread | forced; inverted | the two lookup tests |
| M7, M9, M10, N1, N2 | a missing expanded key, a list with no value, an object with no id, a missing or null `appRoles` | each check removed | the matching unread tests |
| M8 | the 20-or-more re-read | `-ge` made `-gt` | the three re-read tests |
| M11a to M11c | an object listed twice counts once | each dedupe removed | "counts an object listed twice once" |
| M13 | the sort's casts | removed | the sort tests |
| M14 | the id in a re-read's path URI-escaped (the final review's fix, `Get-OERServicePrincipalAccess.ps1:159` then, `:191` since R-14, mutated in the built module) | `-f $ItemId`, unescaped | the two escape tests |
| N3 to N10 | the grant's two names, and `-Detailed`'s two properties | each changed | the name tests |
| C1, C2 | `ConvertTo-OERPrincipalType`: the optional prefix; the ordinal comparison | removed; culture-based | the prefix cases; the culture case |
| R1 to R3, P1 | README section, label sentence and label; prompt bullet, each only with the switch or entry | forced on, or the label branch removed | the byte-identity and label tests |
| E1 to E8 | the export: reader not called without the switch, null-not-`[]`, `IncompleteReads` (output and README), `InventoryPartial` trigger, a reader that stops, the parameters and the file only with the switch | each removed or forced | the export's switch tests |
| RS1, RS2 | the requiredscope `applications` and `oauth2PermissionGrants` rules | each made to match nothing | 4 and 3 red, the case for the export's literals among them |
| RS3, RS4 | the same two rules narrowed so `Directory.Read.All` does not satisfy them | `Read` narrowed | the export's per-cmdlet case red, naming the literals |
| RS5 | `Directory.Read.All` in the export's row of `Get-OERRequiredScopeMap` | dropped (rebuilt) | the export's per-cmdlet case red, 20 unsatisfied, 8 of them the reader's |
| L1, L12 to L14 | check 1.1: an expanded entry without an id its row needs is read in full (`:188`, and `-RequiredKey` at each of the three calls) | the condition removed; each `-RequiredKey` dropped | 12 red; 8, 2 and 2 red (the re-read tests of that part) |
| L2, L3 | `Get-MissingKey`: a blank id is missing (`:171`) | `IsNullOrEmpty`; never missing | the 4 blank-id tests; 12 red |
| L4, L5, L15 | R-14: an assignment the full read returns without its ids leaves `applicationPermissions` `null`, with its cause (`:262`, `:276`, `:118`) | the check forced off; the rows built anyway; the two key words swapped | the 3 "leaves only the application permissions unread" tests |
| L6, L7 | R-14: the list goes on and the grants are read (`:267`, `:384`) | `continue` made `break`; the old gate on `applicationPermissions` | the same 3 tests (the grants' resource name; the grants unread) |
| L8, L9 | the list-read flag (`:298`, `:230`) | never set; set before the read | 40 red; the 7 tests of a failed service principal list |
| L10, L11 | an owner the full read returns without an id leaves that part unread (`:322`, `:359`) | each check removed | the unread test of that part |

### CLAUDE.md text for service-principal-access

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Get-OERServicePrincipalAccess` is the single reader of what `servicePrincipalAccess.json`
  holds** (Sprint 11 step 8, A7): the service principal list with `$expand=appRoleAssignments` (the
  application permissions, read from the client side), the service principal and app registration
  lists with `$expand=owners(...)`, and one paged `oauth2PermissionGrants` list whose users it looks
  up with ONE `Resolve-OERPrincipalName -Detailed` call. An object whose expanded collection holds
  20 or more entries, or one of whose expanded entries lacks the id its row needs (an app role
  assignment without `resourceId` or `appRoleId`, an owner without `id`), is read again in full with
  a paged read of its own, since Microsoft Graph documents at most 20 for an expanded directory
  relationship and was measured to return an expanded app role assignment with a null `resourceId`.
  An app role assignment the full read still returns without them leaves only
  `applicationPermissions` unread (R-14). A part is read whole or not at all: any failure inside it
  leaves it `$null`, never `[]`, and names it `servicePrincipalAccess/<part>`; the grants are not
  read when the service principal list was not. It never throws, never writes an error record or a
  warning, and sends GET requests only, with no `-Method` (the requiredscope gate would judge every
  literal of a function that writes as a write). `Export-OERInventory` calls it once, only with
  `-IncludeServicePrincipalAccess` (A9), and nothing reads the file back: never add its content to
  `inventory.json`, `schema.json` or the apply engine. **`ConvertTo-OERPrincipalType` is the single
  owner of mapping a Microsoft Graph object type to the document's principal type** (`User`, `Group`
  or `ServicePrincipal`, the `#microsoft.graph.` prefix optional, letter case ignored; anything else
  `$null`, never guessed), used for the owner rows and for the `principalType` `Get-OERInventory`
  writes on an `administrativeUnits[].scopedRoles` row whose principal the directory returned.
  `ConvertTo-OERDirectoryRoleAssignment` keeps the mapping it had before this one (a named
  exception, not a precedent); never map a Graph type inline anywhere else. The validator holds the
  scoped role `principalType` to the enum and `Read-OERStructureDocument` canonicalises it, but
  `Sync-OERStructureAdministrativeUnit` never uses it to match or write.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#service-principal-access`,
  `docs/development/rationale.md#scoped-role-principal-type`

## scoped-role-principal-type

Sprint 11 step 8 writes `principalType` on an `administrativeUnits[].scopedRoles` row. A Graph scoped
role membership names its member by id and does not say what kind of object it is, so a scoped role
row named only a principal, and a reader of the document could not tell a user from a group or a
service principal. No ErrorId and no public parameter was added.

**The read.** After the unit loop, `Get-OERInventory` collects the distinct principals that are object
ids (`Test-OERGuid`) over every unit's rows, and, when there is at least one, looks them up ONCE through
`Resolve-OERPrincipalName -Detailed` (one `getByIds` request per 1,000 ids), into answers of the
section's own: the shared name cache is not read or written. A row whose principal the directory
returned as a user, a group or a service principal gets `principalType` after `principal`, in the
casing `ConvertTo-OERPrincipalType` gives. A principal the directory did not return, one of another
type (a device, for one) and one named by its display name keep their row as it is, and nothing is
reported: the type is information. A lookup that did not read, or an id it gave no answer for, leaves
the rows of those principals without the key and names each such unit unread ONCE, as
`administrativeUnits/<name>/scopedRoles/principalType`, with the cause of its first such principal.
Since one batch can fail while another succeeds, a named unit can hold rows with the key and rows
without it -- "some or all of its rows", as every text says. The `scopedRoles` collection itself was
read, so it stays written: the entry names no null collection, which the `InventoryPartial` message of
`Get-OERInventory` says in a sentence of its own, and the bundle README adds a paragraph for such an
entry only when one is present (the README's other prose stays as it was). The export's message has
no such sentence since Sprint 11 step 14 (BL-156): it names the entries and points at the bundle
README, whose paragraph on a `/scopedRoles/principalType` entry is the export's account of it.

**The document.** The schema declares the key optional, the enum `User`, `Group`, `ServicePrincipal`.
Ruling R-7: the validator holds it to the enum, as it does a role assignment's -- a value outside it is
an Error, another letter case a Warning -- and `Read-OERStructureDocument` canonicalises it, so the
Warning's "Invoke-OERStructure normalizes the casing" stays true. `Sync-OERStructureAdministrativeUnit`
is unchanged: it matches a scoped role by role and principal, so it never uses the key to match or
write. So the texts say "does not use it to match or write", never "does not read it", since the
reader and the validator do. A round trip holds it: a mocked live unit with a user, a group and a
service principal exported with the real `Get-OERInventory` and applied with the real
`Invoke-OERStructure` is `Unchanged` for every scoped role, with and without `-Prune`, and so is the
same document with every `principalType` swapped to another type; a control without one row removes
exactly that membership under `-Prune`. Cost if wrong (R-7): a hand-written document with a wrong
`principalType` on a scoped role is refused although apply would ignore the key.

**Known limits.** (a) The validator accepted an array `principalType` such as `["User"]`, as it did for
`roleAssignments` (a pre-existing pattern), until Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-155) made a value that is not a
string an Error in both sections ([#enum-values-must-be-strings](#enum-values-must-be-strings)). (b) A unit later left out of the document because another
unit shares its name is looked up, and named unread when the lookup failed, all the same. (c) The
`InventoryPartial` sentence about such an entry stands in every partial message of `Get-OERInventory`
(since Sprint 11 step 14 (BL-156) no longer in the export's, which points at the bundle README), also
when no such entry is listed; the bundle README's paragraph does not.

**Mutation proofs.** Task 2 of the step (the inventory, the validator, the reader), each against a
build; Task 4 (the README sentence) against a dev-mode copy of the source, where the unmutated copy
ran 160 of 160 green. Every mutant turned at least one test red.

| Id | Guard | Mutant | Red |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1, M3 | `Found`, and a type the mapping names | each removed | the principalType row test |
| M2, M14 | a lookup that did not read, or gave no answer, is unread | each loosened | the failed-lookup and no-answer tests |
| M4 | one batch for every unit | one call per id | the single-batch and failed-lookup tests |
| M5, M6, M7, M8 | no lookup when no object id; object ids only, distinct, per row | each removed | the no-lookup, single-batch and row tests |
| M9, M10, M11, M12, M13 | the unread entry, once per unit, with the first cause | each removed or forced | the failed-lookup, first-cause and no-answer tests |
| V1, V2, V3 | the validator's enum Error, casing Warning, only when declared | each removed or forced | the validator's enum, casing and no-key tests |
| R1 | the reader's canonicalisation | removed | both reader tests |
| T1, T5 | the README sentence only when such an entry is present | `if ($true)`; `if ($false)` | 4 red each: the four "adds no sentence" cases; the three "adds the sentence" cases and the order test |
| T2 | only for an Entra ID entry | the label condition removed | 2 red: the role assignment principal entry and the Azure scope |
| T3, T4 | the path at the end of the entry or before a comma | the anchor dropped; the end alone | 1 red (a path that only starts the same way); 2 red (the comma cases) |

## failed-policy-read

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-40, rulings R-1 and R-2): a live read whose answer decides what the apply engine
writes is never taken as "nothing there".

**What was wrong.** `Sync-OERStructureRoleManagementPolicy` read the live Azure role management policy
without `-ErrorAction Stop`. `Get-OERRoleManagementPolicy` writes its failures as non-terminating errors
-- a role definition it cannot find, a policy assignment list Azure Resource Manager refuses -- so such
a read returned nothing, the handler's catch never ran, and the diff, handed no current policy, took
every declared field as changed. For an entry that declared only `approvers.users`, the side it did not
declare was seeded from that missing policy as empty, so the write could replace the live group
approvers with none, and a `-WhatIf` plan said "would update".

**What it does now.** The read carries `-ErrorAction Stop`, so the catch -- scrub first, the record
published as itself through `$Caller.WriteError`, a `Failed` row carrying it -- runs for every failure,
and a read that returns no policy and no error is refused too (`PolicyNotFound`, category
`ObjectNotFound`, the role and scope as target). Both stand before the approver lookup, the diff, the
`ApproverRequired` check and `ShouldProcess`, so a `-WhatIf` plan reports the same row and nothing is
written. `Resolve-OERRoleManagementPolicyChange` is unchanged: its branch for a missing current policy
serves a direct caller only, and its help says a caller refuses a failed or empty read first.

**The sweep (R-2).** Every read of live state in every `Sync-OERStructure*` handler and in the engine,
35 reads, was audited for the same shape, and one more had it: the group `pimPolicy` read in step 4 of
`Sync-OERStructureGroup`, whose catch swallowed the error and left the current policy unset. The diff
then sent every declared field and defaulted the undeclared half of a duration pair: an
`eligibleDurationDays` declared alone also sent `allowPermanentEligibility` false, whatever the policy
had. That read now ends its access type with a `Failed` row carrying the read's own record
(`PimPolicyNotFound` for a read that returned no policy and no error), before the diff, the PIM-in-use
question, the conflict warning and `ShouldProcess`, in a run and under `-WhatIf`, and the other access
type is processed as usual. Every other read already ended in a `Failed` row or a throw to the engine,
or only stops a write or a prune. The directory role handler also reads with `-ErrorAction Stop`; it
has no empty-answer guard of its own, since `Get-OERDirectoryRoleManagementPolicy -Role` writes an
error on every path that returns no policy.

**The tests.** Context "a failed read of the live policy never feeds a write (BL-40)" in
`Sync-OERStructureRoleManagementPolicy.Tests.ps1` and Context "a failed or empty read of the live
pimPolicy never feeds a write (BL-40)" in `Sync-OERStructureGroup.Tests.ps1` drive four read shapes --
a non-terminating mock, the real cmdlet failing non-terminating, a terminating failure, and no answer
-- in a run and under `-WhatIf`, with the global `$ErrorActionPreference` pinned to Continue, so a CI
Stop preference cannot hide a missing `-ErrorAction Stop`. Two Describes in
`Invoke-OERStructure.Tests.ps1` run the public engine in a runspace with no `try`. Cost if R-1 is
wrong: a second guard belongs in the diff.

### An unread directory role name map stops only the scopedRoles (BL-47, R-7)

When the document declares a scoped role by its role id and the unit holds a live scoped role named
by the directory, `Sync-OERStructureAdministrativeUnit` reads the directory role list a second time
(`Get-OERDirectoryRoleNameMap -ThrowOnFailure`) to match the two through the role's other id. When that
read failed, the handler returned at once and the whole unit was `Failed`, its properties and members
included. Now the read's record (`AdministrativeUnitScopedRoleReadFailed`, `ReadError`, the unit id as
target, its message ending "No scopedRole change was made.") is written once, at the read; the
properties and members are applied as usual, in a run and under `-WhatIf`; and the scopedRoles step,
the last of the handler, reports one `Failed` row carrying that record and returns, with no principal
lookup, no add, no removal and no `Extra` row, with or without `-Prune`. The scopedRoles collection is
the smallest part that can be stopped without a wrong write: without the map, a role declared by id
that matches a live role through its other id would be added a second time and its live entry pruned.
The first read of the role list, inside `Get-OERAdministrativeUnit -IncludeScopedRoles`, still fails
the whole unit as an unread scoped-role collection. The record is written at the read and not in the
guard (ruled): under a Stop preference a write in the guard would throw after the property and member
writes and lose their rows. So a unit whose rename fails, which returns before the scopedRoles step,
shows the map's record beside the rename's own `Failed` row and no scopedRoles row. Cost if wrong: a
scoped role declared by name waits one run.

## last-user-owner

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-84, ruling R-15).

**Measured.** In the test tenant on 2026-10-20 (check 1.2 of
`docs/live-verification/fix-engine-and-validator-findings-checklist.md`), Microsoft Graph refused to
remove a group's only user owner while a service principal was its other owner: the `DELETE` of the
owner reference answered 400 `Request_BadRequest`, "The group must have at least one owner, hence this
owner cannot be removed.", and the owners were unchanged. A service principal owner does not stand in
for the last user owner.

**What the engine did.** The owner prune pass of `Sync-OERStructureGroup` held back only the last
remaining owner of any type, and counted a service principal owner, which `-Prune` never removes, as an
owner standing. So with one user owner and one service principal owner, and no owner declared,
`-Prune` sent a removal of the user owner that Graph refuses.

**What it does now.** A user-owner floor is asked first: an undeclared owner whose `ObjectType` is
`user` (in any letter case) and who is the last user owner still standing is never removed -- `Skipped`,
with a Detail that quotes the measurement, and no warning, no `ShouldProcess` and no request. The floor
for the last owner of any type stays, reached now only by an owner not typed user, and its text no
longer says "pending live verification". A withheld owner (an unresolved entry, a service principal, a
synchronized group, an unread or a held PIM state) still counts as standing, and a withheld user owner
as a user owner. A removal that went through lowers the count of owners standing, and a user owner's
removal the count of user owners too; one that failed, or was declined at the confirmation prompt,
leaves its owner standing. A `-WhatIf` plan counts each removal it reports as
done, so it holds back the same owner a run does; before that fix, a plan for two undeclared user owners
said "would remove" for both while the run refused the second. An owner with no `ObjectType` is not
counted as a user owner (the typed read carries one in a real tenant). Context "the last user owner is
never removed, also while a service principal is an owner (BL-84, R-15)" in
`Sync-OERStructureGroup.Tests.ps1` holds it. Cost if wrong: a removal Graph would have accepted waits
for the operator.

**An owner the same run adds counts as standing** (final review of the step, probe P1). The floors
first counted only the owners the read found, so a document that swapped the user owner of a group
with a service principal owner (live: one user and the service principal; declared: another user)
added the new user and then refused to remove the old one as "the last remaining user owner", which
was false: the new user stood, and Graph would have accepted the removal; before the user floor that
swap completed in one run. A single owner replaced by another was held back the same way by the
any-type floor, a flaw older than the user floor. Now an owner the add pass added counts in the
any-type count, and in the user count when the declared-owner resolution knows it is a user -- a
reference with an at sign, which `Resolve-OERStructurePrincipal` resolves as a user principal name.
An owner named any other way, by object id for one, names no type, so it counts in the any-type
count only: the conservative reading, which can still hold back the last user owner beside it. A
`-WhatIf` plan counts an owner it reports "would add", as it counts a removal it reports; an add
that failed, or one declined at the confirmation prompt, counts nowhere.
Each owner is counted once by its id, so a reference declared twice cannot count twice. Cost if wrong:
an owner added by object id beside the last user owner leaves that removal to a later run.

## unknown-allowed-target-scope

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-49, decision A24, ruling R-13).

**Measured.** Microsoft Graph answers an access package assignment policy's `allowedTargetScope` with
`unknownFutureValue` for a value of the enumeration it names only when the request carries the header
`Prefer: include-unknown-enum-members`, which this module never sends. In the test tenant on 2026-10-20
(check 1.1 of the step's checklist) no policy read back as the placeholder: one created with
`allDirectoryAgentIdentities` read back as itself with and without the header. But a PUT of a policy
with its own read body and `allowedTargetScope` set to `unknownFutureValue` answered 200 and STORED the
placeholder as the policy's scope, read back so with and without the header. A write that carries a
read placeholder back therefore replaces the policy's real scope.

**What the cmdlet does now.** `Set-OERAccessPackageAssignmentPolicy` carries the live scope forward
through `ConvertTo-OERPolicyBody` when `-RequestorScope` is not given. It now refuses, after its one read
and its `NothingToUpdate` and `AccessPackageNotFound` checks and before the body is built,
`ShouldProcess` and the PUT, when `-RequestorScope` is not bound and the policy it read carries
`allowedTargetScope` `unknownFutureValue` in any letter case: the new ErrorId
`UnknownAllowedTargetScope` (A9, a refusal), category `InvalidData`, the policy id as target. It does so
under `-WhatIf` too, and for a rename that changes nothing else. A bound `-RequestorScope` writes as
before, and any other read scope is carried forward as before. The apply engine already refused such a
policy, whatever the entry declares, as a `Failed` row with nothing written
(`Sync-OERStructureAccessPackage`); that is unchanged. Cost if wrong: an operator with such a policy
passes `-RequestorScope` to update it.

## confirmation-unavailable

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-53, ruling R-4). `Test-OERHostCanConfirm` and `Test-OERConfirmPromptFailure` are
the single owners of the two decisions below.

**Measured** on 2026-10-20 in plain PowerShell, with no module code loaded, on a function with
`ConfirmImpact` High called without `-Confirm:$false` and without `-WhatIf`: `ShouldProcess` does not
answer no in a host that cannot ask, it throws a `MethodInvocationException`, whose inner exception is
a `HostException` in the Default Host (a runspace made with `[powershell]::Create()` without a host of
its own, or a thread job, `Start-ThreadJob`), a `PSInvalidOperationException` under
`pwsh -NonInteractive` (and `-noni`), and a `NullReferenceException` with standard input at its end (the
live case of Sprint 8 step 3); with standard input redirected from a pipe that still held input it read
the default answer, yes. `$Host.UI` is never null. `Invoke-OERStructure` runs with `ConfirmImpact` High,
so each handler's `$Caller.ShouldProcess` threw there, and the engine's catch reported the entry
`Failed` with the host's raw message, which did not say what was missing. Only the Default Host can be
told beforehand, by `$Host.Name -eq 'Default Host'`; the other two would need the process command line
or the console's state.

**The Default Host is refused before the sign-in.** When the run would prompt -- not `-WhatIf`, and
`$ConfirmPreference` not `None`, which `-Confirm:$false` sets inside the command -- and
`Test-OERHostCanConfirm` says the host is the Default Host, the document is refused with the new ErrorId
`ConfirmationUnavailable` (A9), category `InvalidOperation`, once it has been read and validated and
before the tenant alias, the Azure Resource Manager decision, both tenant comparisons, the session
snapshot check and `Initialize-OERAuth`: nothing is signed in to, read or written, and the next piped
document is handled the same way. Measured too: inside the command the refusal reads the same
`$ConfirmPreference` and `$WhatIfPreference` that `ShouldProcess` reads -- `-Confirm:$false` makes the
first `None`, `-WhatIf` sets the second, and a global `$ConfirmPreference = 'None'` is seen by both --
so a refused run is one that would have prompted.

**Every other host gets a row that says what is missing.** The engine's two handler-error catches
(`pre-pass handler error` and `handler error`) word the Detail through `Test-OERConfirmPromptFailure`
when the caught record is that failure: a `MethodInvocationException`, its inner exception one of the
three measured types or one derived from them, and its message naming `ShouldProcess` (compared
ordinally). The Detail then says that the host cannot show the confirmation prompt, that nothing was
written for the entry, and to run with `-Confirm:$false` to apply without prompts or with `-WhatIf` to
plan; the record is still published as itself, and every other error keeps its own message. No handler
calls `$Caller.ShouldProcess` inside a `try` of its own, so the failure reaches those catches.

Cost (accepted): a Default Host run that would have changed nothing now needs `-Confirm:$false` or
`-WhatIf`. A host the refusal misses still gets the clear row. The `(BL-53)` Describe of
`Invoke-OERStructure.Tests.ps1` holds it, in a real Default Host runspace with no `try` among others,
beside the two helpers' own test files.

### CLAUDE.md text for confirmation-unavailable

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Test-OERHostCanConfirm` is the single owner of whether the host can show a confirmation prompt
  that is decidable beforehand, and `Test-OERConfirmPromptFailure` of whether a caught record is a
  `ShouldProcess` that failed because the host could not ask** (Sprint 11 step 11, BL-53). The first is
  `$Host.Name -ne 'Default Host'`, the only host the measurement found safely decidable;
  `Invoke-OERStructure` refuses with `ConfirmationUnavailable`, before the sign-in, a document whose run
  would prompt (not `-WhatIf`, `$ConfirmPreference` not `None`) when it answers false. The second is
  true only for a `MethodInvocationException` whose inner exception is a `HostException`,
  `PSInvalidOperationException` or `NullReferenceException` (or derives from one) and whose message
  names `ShouldProcess` (ordinal); the engine's two handler-error catches word the Detail through it.
  Never decide either anywhere else.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#confirmation-unavailable`

## structure-document-text

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-154, ruling R-11). `Test-OERJsonDateKindSupport` is the single owner of whether
the running `ConvertFrom-Json` has `-DateKind`.

**First point: a file that cannot be read says why.** `Read-OERStructureDocument` read the file with
`Get-Content -Raw` and no `-ErrorAction Stop`. For a file it cannot open -- a lock, no read permission --
`Get-Content` writes a non-terminating error and returns nothing, so the operator got that raw error
and then "The structure document is empty." beside it. The read now runs with `-ErrorAction Stop`, and
its catch scrubs the record and throws one error that names the path and the reason, which
`Test-OERStructure` and `Invoke-OERStructure` publish as `InvalidStructureDocument`, as
`Read-OERNamingStandard` already reports an unreadable standard.

**Second point: the text stays as written.** `ConvertFrom-Json` turns a string that holds an ISO 8601
date and time with seconds into a `DateTime` while it parses, and leaves a date alone or a time without
seconds a string (the forms are measured under [#naming-standard](#naming-standard)), so a `startDate`
or an `expirationDateTime` written with such a time, or a `displayName` that looks like a time stamp,
reached the validator and the apply engine as a date, not as the text written. PowerShell
7.5 added `-DateKind`, and `-DateKind String` leaves every string as written. The reader adds it whenever
`ConvertFrom-Json` has the parameter, which `Test-OERJsonDateKindSupport` decides with one `Get-Command`
of the module-qualified `Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\ConvertFrom-Json`, so a function the caller defines
under that name is never the one asked. PowerShell 7.2 to 7.4 has no such parameter, and the module does
not try to undo the conversion: the validator refuses instead (Rule 2b). Every `DateTime` or
`DateTimeOffset` value in the document, at any depth, is an `Error` at its own path that says the value
was read as a date, not as the text written, and to run on PowerShell 7.5 or later. So on those versions
a document with such a string anywhere -- an assignment policy's `expirationDateTime`, which carries a
time, for example -- is refused by `Test-OERStructure` and `Invoke-OERStructure`; no field is exempted
(ruled), since an exemption would let a converted value through. A date alone stays a string on every
version. On PowerShell 7.5 or later an `-InputObject` whose values the caller already turned into dates
is read as `ConvertTo-Json` writes them, a documented limit; on 7.2 to 7.4 those values come back as
dates from the re-parse and are refused like any other.

**`displayName` must be a string.** In `groups`, `administrativeUnits`, `catalogs`, `accessPackages`,
`assignmentPolicies` and `accessReviews`, a `displayName` that is a number, a boolean, an object or an
array is an `Error` at its path naming the type found; a date gets only the date `Error`. With a naming
standard, Rule 17 adds a `Warning` that such a name was not checked, a date included.

Cost if wrong: a user on PowerShell 7.2 to 7.4 has to run 7.5 or later to apply a document that holds a
date and time with seconds; nothing is ever changed on the way. Held by `Read-OERStructureDocument.Tests.ps1`,
`Test-OERJsonDateKindSupport.Tests.ps1`, the date and displayName Contexts of
`Test-OERStructureSchema.Tests.ps1`, and a runspace with no `try` in `Invoke-OERStructure.Tests.ps1`
with `Test-OERJsonDateKindSupport` stubbed false.

### CLAUDE.md text for structure-document-text

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **`Test-OERJsonDateKindSupport` is the single owner of whether the running `ConvertFrom-Json` has
  `-DateKind`** (Sprint 11 step 11, BL-154): one `Get-Command` of the module-qualified
  `Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\ConvertFrom-Json`, true when it has the parameter (PowerShell 7.5 or
  later). `Read-OERStructureDocument` adds `-DateKind String` to its parse when it answers true, so a
  structure document reaches the validator and the engine as written; on PowerShell 7.2 to 7.4
  `Test-OERStructureSchema` refuses every date value the parse made (Rule 2b), with no field exempted.
  Never ask the question anywhere else, and never "repair" a parsed date into text. A test mocks it in
  module scope to run the 7.2 to 7.4 path on a newer PowerShell.
  `Why: docs/development/rationale.md#structure-document-text`

## naming-template-one-pass

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-139, ruling R-12).

`Resolve-OERName` substituted with one `-replace` per token, so each value was a replacement string: a
`$` sequence in it was read as a substitution (`$&`, `$$`, `$_`, `${name}` and the like), and a value that looked like
another token could be replaced again by a later pass, depending on the order the keys came in. It now
reads the template once, with `[regex]::Replace` and an evaluator over `{token}`, and inserts each
value as text: a `$` in a value is never interpreted, and a value is never read again as a token.
Token names are still matched ignoring letter case (an `OrdinalIgnoreCase` dictionary, also for a
case-sensitive hashtable). The unresolved tokens are the template's own, in template order, with the
same message for the same input; `-MaxLength` and `-Strict` are unchanged. Two edges follow from the
expression and are pinned by tests: `{{a}` with a key `a` is unresolved as `{a`, and `{}` stays `{}`.

The validator reports a group template that cannot be resolved -- a placeholder no token supplies (an
empty or null token value resolves, to an empty text), a name over
256 characters -- as an `Error` at `groups[i].template` carrying `Resolve-OERName`'s reason, when the
entry declares no `displayName`. Before, `Test-OERStructure` raised nothing for it and
`Invoke-OERStructure` reported that group `Failed` at apply; now the whole document is refused before
anything is read or written, since the apply would fail for it anyway. The Error is computed from the
tokens the engine would pass, so a missing `tokens` gives it beside the `tokens` Error. Cost if wrong:
a token value that holds `{x}` is kept as text instead of being reported unresolved.

## enum-values-must-be-strings

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-155 third point, BL-117 fifth point). The `principalType` of a `roleAssignments`
entry and of an `administrativeUnits[].scopedRoles` entry, and the `recurrence` of an `accessReviews`
entry, were checked with `-inotcontains` against the canonical list, which lets a one-element array
such as `["User"]` through, since the comparison reads the array as the string it holds. Each is now an
`Error` unless it is a string in the list, and the message names the type of a value that is not a
string ("a value that is not a string (Object[])"), worded by one local helper in the validator that the
`principalStatus` and `principal` texts share, with their output unchanged. The same hole remains in a
few other enums (a `directoryRoleAssignments` `principalType`, an access review's `defaultDecision`,
`approverInfoVisibility`, a catalog resource `type`, and the enums cast to `[string]`), recorded as a
finding for a later step.

## validator-warnings-for-graph-refusals

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-54, BL-24).

**An Any User policy without approval (BL-54).** Microsoft Graph refuses an assignment policy whose
`requestorScope.scope` is `AllExternalUsers` -- the option its message calls Any User -- and that has
no approval configured: `AnyUserPolicyValidationError`, "An access package policy with Any User option
must have an approval configured". The validator warns at
`accessPackages[i].assignmentPolicies[k].requestorScope.scope` (the scope read ignoring letter case)
unless the entry declares at least one `approvalStages` entry and does not declare `requireApproval`
false. With `requireApproval` left out the apply derives it from the stage count, so a stage alone is
approval (ruled: a Warning there would be false). One text names a `requireApproval` false; the other
names the missing stage and says what the engine does with what the entry leaves out, in one of three
clauses. With `requireApproval` left out, an existing policy keeps its live approval settings, so the
update is accepted only when the live policy already requires approval with a stage. With
`requireApproval` true declared, only the live stages matter. With `approvalStages` declared empty, the
empty list is sent, so the write carries no stage whatever the live policy has, and a refusal is
expected: Microsoft Graph's answer to that combination is not measured, and the text says so. A
Warning, never an Error, since the validator cannot see the live policy.

**A GUID as an access package name (BL-24).** An `accessPackages` `displayName` that is a canonical
GUID (`Test-OERGuid`) is a Warning at its path: the engine creates the package with that name, and an
access review or another reference that names it reads the GUID as an object id. The other BL-24 point,
the directory role guard's "eligible for" wording, is under
[#directory-role-assignments](#directory-role-assignments).

## run-right-after-a-write

Sprint 11 step 11 (BL-121, second point): documented, no code.

Measured in Sprint 10 step 7b (check 3.2 of
`docs/live-verification/feat-show-and-export-synced-groups-checklist.md`): after a group description
PATCH, Microsoft Graph answered the apply engine's read with the description from before the PATCH
for a while -- with no wait, after the read by name had converged, and after three matching reads by id
within 7 seconds -- while ten paired reads 25 seconds later all matched. An apply started within about
30 seconds of a write can therefore find the change the previous run made still missing and send the
same update again. The update is idempotent -- it writes the value already written and changes nothing
more -- but its row reads `Updated` again instead of `Unchanged`, so two runs in quick succession do not
prove convergence. A run after the reads settle reports `Unchanged`, and the live checklists wait for
that before a convergence check. The help of `Invoke-OERStructure` says so. Cost: none in the tenant; a
row that overstates the second run.

Working rules for this repo. This file carries **rules**; the history behind them lives in

## branch-policy

This section records the CLAUDE.md text on the branch policy and the merge requirements on `main` as it stood before step 11b.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

**`main` is protected on GitHub and a direct push to it is REJECTED BY THE SERVER.** That is
deliberate. It is not a lock to be worked around, and "continue on the current branch" is no longer
an option a user can consent to on `main` -- consent does not move a server-side rule. Every change
reaches `main` through a pull request.

**Before making any code change, Claude must:**

2. If the current branch is `main`, create a feature branch before touching any files:
   `git checkout -b <branch-name>`, named from the table below. Propose the name and say what it is
   for; do not stop and wait for permission to leave `main`, since staying there cannot produce a
   push.

3. If the current branch is some OTHER shared branch, stop and ask the user which branch to use --
   there the old rule still holds, because the push would succeed.

**Merge requirements, enforced by GitHub on `main` (as measured on 2026-10-08):**

- **Four status checks are required: `ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest`, `macos-latest` and
  `package`.** The first three come from the build-and-test matrix's `name: ${{ matrix.os }}`, so
  the job name IS the required check name -- renaming the job, or changing the matrix, orphans the
  protection rule and blocks every open PR until the rule is renamed to match. `package` is the
  `package` job's own `name: package` in the same workflow: the job that runs after all three legs
  (`needs: build-and-test`) and proves on the pull request that the artefact is publishable,
  without publishing it. Renaming its `name:` (or, with `name:` removed, its job id, which the check
  name then falls back to) orphans the fourth rule the same way. Change both together.

- **`package` never holds the gate alone.** It has no `if:` of its own, so when a leg fails or is
  skipped GitHub skips `package` too, and a skipped check counts as passed ("Troubleshooting
  required status checks": successful statuses are `success`, `skipped` and `neutral`). The three
  leg checks are what stop a red pull request, so never drop them from the rule in favour of
  `package`.

- **The branch must be up to date with `main` before it can merge** (the rule is strict). A branch
  that has fallen behind is rebased onto `main` and force-pushed; the checks then re-run against the
  rebased tip.

- **Linear history is required**, so a merge commit is refused. Squash merge is the convention here.

- **Every conversation on the PR must be resolved** before merge.

- **The rule binds administrators too** (`enforce_admins` is on), so no account merges past it.

## project-overview

This section records the CLAUDE.md text on what the module is and which clone is canonical as it stood before step 11b.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

`Omnicit.EntraRBAC` is a PowerShell 7.2+ (Core-only) module built and maintained by Omnicit AB. MIT
licensed and **published on the public PowerShell Gallery for anyone to use**: 1.0.0 went out by
hand on 2026-09-18, and everything since publishes itself -- see **Publishing** below.

It manages RBAC building blocks across many Entra ID and Azure tenants: Entra ID groups, PIM,
Administrative Units, Entitlement Management, Access Reviews, Azure resources and RBAC, plus a JSON
inventory and a declarative apply engine. Command prefix is `OER`.

**The canonical working tree is the clone whose `origin` is
`github.com/Omnicit/Omnicit.EntraRBAC`**, wherever it sits on disk. The local path differs from
machine to machine, so identify it with `git remote get-url origin`, never by its directory. The
older clone, whose `origin` is the private repository, is to be archived; do not commit to it, and
do not treat a change made there as made. Two live clones of one module is how a fix lands in the
wrong repository -- that has already happened here.

The phase roadmap (phases 0-5) is **complete** -- the module is feature-complete. See `CHANGELOG.md`
for what each release delivered.

## required-checks-and-the-matrix

This section records the CLAUDE.md text on why the build-and-test job condition is wired to the merge gate, and why the matrix matters, as it stood before step 11b.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

**The build-and-test job's `if:` condition is now wired to the merge gate -- do not read it as a
billing guard alone, and do not reason about it from GitHub's general rule for skipped jobs.** The
job is declared
`if: ${{ !github.event.repository.private || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' }}`, because
standard runners are free and unmetered only on a PUBLIC repository. `ubuntu-latest`,
`windows-latest`, `macos-latest` and `package` are the four REQUIRED checks on `main`, and that
condition decides whether the first three ever come into existence; `package` follows them through
`needs: build-and-test`.

**The mechanism is the MATRIX, not the skip.** GitHub documents the opposite of what happens here:
a job skipped by a condition reports Success and does NOT block a pull request ("Troubleshooting
required status checks"). That rule does not rescue this workflow, because `build-and-test` is a
matrix job and a job-level `if:` is evaluated BEFORE the matrix expands. The three legs are
therefore never created, so nothing ever reports the three check names -- and a required check that
never reports stays pending forever instead of passing (community discussion #9141). The fourth
check does not change that: `package` is skipped with the job it needs, and a skipped check counts
as passed, but the three matrix names still never report. Make this repository private again and
every pull request blocks permanently, including the pull request that would fix it. Turning the
repository private is therefore a change to this condition, or to the protection rule, made in the
SAME change and never afterwards.

**Rewriting this workflow as three separate jobs without a matrix INVERTS the failure, into the
worse one.** Without a matrix there is nothing to expand: the job-level `if:` would then skip three
jobs that do exist, each would report Success under the documented rule, and the merge gate would
go GREEN having run not one test -- `package` included, since it would be skipped with them. The
matrix is what makes a skip fail loudly here, so keep it -- or, if the jobs are ever split, make the
required checks something a skipped job cannot satisfy.

## qa-gates

This section records the CLAUDE.md text on the Markdown, docsync and cross-cutting test suite gates as it stood before step 11b.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

**`dochygiene.tests.ps1` also reads Markdown the way GitHub renders it.** In every tracked `.md`
under `docs/` and `specs/`, and in `README.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` at the root, no angle bracket
that looks like a tag (`<word>`, `</word>`, `<!...>`, `<?...>`) may stand outside code: GitHub
renders it as nothing, so a redacted `<id>` stand-in vanishes from the record. `CHANGELOG.md`'s
`[Unreleased]` also becomes the GitHub release body (the publish job's `gh release create
--notes-file`), which GitHub renders the same way and hides the bracket too -- but the PowerShell
Gallery shows those same notes as HTML-encoded plain text, where a bracket is SHOWN, not hidden,
and a backslash escape would show there too, permanently. So in `CHANGELOG.md` use backticks only,
never a backslash. Elsewhere, write the token inside backticks, or as `\<id>` where a backtick
would close a code span the line already has; quotes alone do not escape it. An autolink
(`<https://...>`) or deliberate inline HTML (`<br>`) is refused the same way, since the check is
exactly the reference algorithm -- write a bare URL instead, or put the markup in backticks. Fenced
blocks and code spans are skipped with the algorithm documented in
`ConvertTo-DocHygieneMarkdownProse`'s own `.DESCRIPTION`, in `tests/QA/dochygiene.tests.ps1`. That
algorithm is the maintainer's `Test-MdAngleBrackets.py`, a script kept outside this repository that
the gate follows where the two differ (the gate's own comment says so), and deliberately not
CommonMark's: never "correct" it towards CommonMark, and carry a change made on either side to the
other, so the two keep agreeing hit for hit.

**`docsync.tests.ps1` holds `README.md` and the about topic against each other.** Each already had
its own "names every exported cmdlet" check, but both matched the whole FILE, so a cmdlet mentioned
only in a Quick Start snippet passed while missing from the roster. This gate scopes the roster to
`## Available Cmdlets` and `COMMAND COHORTS`, checks each `### Cohort (N)` count against the cmdlets
that cohort is the FIRST to name, and requires the two documents to agree word for word on the
tenant-switch verdict per sign-in type and on the device-code known limitation. It also holds every
sentence in either whole document that says "all N cmdlets" or "all N exported cmdlets" -- README's
introduction and `## Available Cmdlets`, the about topic's LONG DESCRIPTION -- to the count of
`FunctionsToExport`, with a floor on the matches so a reworded sentence cannot make it vacuous; a
count written another way ("98 cmdlets" with no "all", a spelled-out number) is not seen. It
deliberately does NOT bind the surrounding prose -- the sovereign-cloud, tenant-profile and
permissions sections are rewritten per medium on purpose.

**Test files named after no single function.** Ten cross-cutting suites exist. Do **NOT** delete
any of them as an orphan when auditing the one-test-file-per-function invariant:

- `Unit/Private/BasePathDefault.Cohort.Tests.ps1` -- asserts all seven `-BasePath`/`-ProfileBasePath`
  default carriers resolve cross-platform (issue #40). It sits under `Private/` because five of the
  seven carriers are public and two are private, so it belongs to neither cohort exclusively. Do not
  "fix" its location by moving it.

- `Unit/Public/AmbiguousName.Guard.Tests.ps1` -- asserts every public call site of an
  ambiguity-refusing `Resolve-OER*Id` helper surfaces the candidate ids instead of a first match.

- `Unit/Public/NothingToUpdate.Cohort.Tests.ps1` -- asserts every `Set-OER*` cmdlet (all twelve)
  reports the no-updatable-property condition as `NothingToUpdate`, and that
  `Set-OERRoleManagementPolicy`'s separate "no rule differs" case keeps its distinct `NoChange` id.

- `Unit/Public/GroupAliasOrder.Cohort.Tests.ps1` -- AST-driven: asserts every `source/Public/*Group*.ps1`
  file declaring a `-Group` parameter lists the `GroupId` alias before the generic `Id` alias, so a
  piped principal can never mis-bind as the piped group.

- `Unit/Public/AdministrativeUnitAliasOrder.Cohort.Tests.ps1` -- the same AST-driven pattern for every
  `-AdministrativeUnit` parameter, so a piped member's own `Id`/`DisplayName` can never mis-bind as
  the piped parent unit.

- `Unit/Public/TenantIdNotEmpty.Cohort.Tests.ps1` -- AST-driven: asserts every public cmdlet that
  declares `-TenantId` carries `[ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]` on it, except `Connect-OER`, whose
  `-TenantId` must carry no validation so its own `InvalidTenantId` refusal runs after the
  session-uncertain marker is set (A12, BL-94); it also drives the binding refusal for the cmdlets
  the live checklist uses. It imports the module, so it installs the transport tripwire.

- `Unit/Public/DirectoryRoleInventory.RoundTrip.Tests.ps1` -- exports the two directory sections
  (`directoryRoleManagementPolicies`, `directoryRoleAssignments`) from a mocked live state with
  `Get-OERInventory` and applies them back through `Invoke-OERStructure`, with and without `-Prune`,
  asserting every row is `Unchanged`. It runs with a session -- a state the test sets for one
  tenant, `Initialize-OERAuth` mocked -- so the export names that tenant (`tenantId`) and the apply
  compares it; the export applied under another tenant is refused with `DocumentTenantMismatch`,
  reading and writing nothing.

- `Unit/Public/WarningBeforeConfirmation.Cohort.Tests.ps1` -- AST-driven: asserts no
  `source/Public/*.ps1` file writes a `Write-Warning` after its first `$PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess`,
  except the warnings its allowlist names with a reason (an entry matching no warning, or two, fails
  too); pins by name and text the twenty cmdlets that warn before their gate; and proves each moved
  warning at run time on `OERConfirmHost`, before the `What if:` line and before the `-Confirm`
  prompt, with no write request. `OER_COHORT_SOURCE_ROOT` points its AST parts at a mutated copy of
  `source/` and is never set in CI (the cadence scan in `Get-OERAccessReviewCadence.Tests.ps1`, the
  `TenantIdNotEmpty` cohort and the scan in `Get-OERGroupRelation.Tests.ps1` read the same
  variable). It imports the module, so it installs the transport tripwire.

- `Unit/TestHelpers/OERTransportTripwire.Tests.ps1` -- the transport tripwire's known-answer suite:
  the six names, resolution from the module scope, parameter parity, mock precedence, the record
  and the refusal, a re-import, the `AfterAll` check, the answering runspace and the uninstall.

### Long runs bound by docsync (Sprint 11 step 15, BL-119)

The quote above is what CLAUDE.md said before step 11b and is left as it was.
`docsync.tests.ps1` also binds the four rows of the Long runs table (what a renewal costs per
sign-in type) in README's `### Long runs` and the about topic's `LONG RUNS`, word for word. Pipes,
backticks, bold, links and line wrapping are normalised away first. The about topic's table has two columns at fixed
positions, so its wrapped label ("Client secret" over "and certificate") is read apart from the text
column and joined as one label. The one cross-reference, to the SWITCHING TENANTS section, is
compared ignoring case, since the about topic names a section in capitals and README in a heading's
case; every other word is compared ordinally. A row missing from either document fails on its own,
so two documents that both lost a row are not reported as agreeing. Known limit: a Markdown link is
reduced to its text, so its anchor target is not compared.

## build-and-test-commands

This section records the CLAUDE.md text on the build and test commands, with the measured coverage, as it stood before step 11b.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

```powershell
# Bootstrap build dependencies (first time or after a clean clone)
./build.ps1 -ResolveDependency -Tasks noop

# If that fails with "Requested value 'V2' was not found" (PSResourceGet compat error), add:
./build.ps1 -ResolveDependency -Tasks noop -UseModuleFast

# Build the module (output lands in output/module/Omnicit.EntraRBAC/<ver>/)
./build.ps1 -Tasks build

# Full test suite -- the authoritative CI gate.
# QA tests + Unit Pester + PSScriptAnalyzer + 80% code coverage enforcement
# (measured 2026-10-08: 94.89% over 18,579 commands, locally on Windows and on all three CI
#  runners of PR #34; macOS measured 94.88% on main's run of bfe1b1a, whose source is the same)
./build.ps1 -Tasks test

# Import from source for quick local development
# (needs AzAuth, Microsoft.Graph.Authentication on PSModulePath;
#  prepend output/RequiredModules if needed)
Import-Module ./source/Omnicit.EntraRBAC.psd1 -Force

# Import the built module
Import-Module ./output/module/Omnicit.EntraRBAC/<ver>/Omnicit.EntraRBAC.psd1 -Force
```

The Sampler test task measures coverage against the **built** module output, not `source/`. Always
run `-Tasks build` before `-Tasks test` after changing source files -- and never build while the
gate is running.

## publishing

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the Publishing rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **A merge that changes only documentation publishes a new preview too.** The workflow has no
  path filter and must not be given one. Accepted in Decision 4 -- a preview per merge is the
  price of the merge-to-main trigger, not a defect to be filtered away.

1. Push `v<X.Y.Z>` on the `main` tip, once that commit's four required checks are green. Only the
   `Stable Version` ruleset's bypass list can create that tag -- as measured on 2026-10-08, the
   Repository admin role and the user PhilipHaglund -- and the push IS the release decision: nothing
   asks for an approval after it. A tag outside the `Entra RBAC` environment's patterns (a major of
   10 or more, or a minor or patch of 100 or more) is refused by the environment, visibly, and
   publishes nothing; the repair is a new pattern the ruleset also covers, never a return to `v*`.

2. Make the close-out the FIRST merge after the tag, exactly as the **close-out after a stable
   release** rule under **CHANGELOG and Version** describes. The invariant to check it against is
   `git show v<X.Y.Z>:CHANGELOG.md` -- the dated section must say what that tag actually shipped.

## tenant-profile-config

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the Tenant Profile Config rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

A profile's optional `Environment` key names the sovereign cloud that tenant lives in (`Global`,
`USGov`, `USGovDoD` or `China`). `Connect-OER -TenantAlias` reads it automatically when the command
line names no `-Environment` of its own, so an operator managing both commercial and sovereign-cloud
tenants does not have to remember, and pass, which is which on every call; an explicit `-Environment`
on the command line always overrides it.

## ascii-only-source-files

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the ASCII-Only Source Files rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

Authored `.ps1` files are UTF-8 **without BOM**. They **must contain only ASCII characters** --
no em-dashes, no box-drawing characters, no smart quotes, no curly apostrophes.

Without a BOM, PowerShell and PSScriptAnalyzer treat the file as ASCII. A non-ASCII character in
a BOM-less file fails the QA `PSUseBOMForUnicodeEncodedFile` PSScriptAnalyzer gate.

The only acceptable exception is a helper file that was verbatim-copied from a source that
already carries a UTF-8 BOM.

Use `--` (two hyphens) for em-dash contexts in comments and help text. Use straight quotes `'`
and `"` only.

## error-handling

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the Error Handling rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **Non-terminating errors** in public functions: `$PSCmdlet.WriteError()` followed by `return` (in
  a `process` block) or `continue` (inside a `foreach` loop over multiple items). Never use bare
  `throw` in a public function -- it terminates the pipeline and prevents
  `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` from working.

- **Private pure helpers** such as `Resolve-OERName` may `throw` on caller error: they have no
  `$PSCmdlet`, and the caller is responsible for catching and routing the error.

- **`Write-CmdletError -Message`** expects an `[Exception]`, not a string. Always wrap bare strings:
  `[System.Exception]::new('message')`.

- **`ErrorDetails` must be set via the constructor** -- plain string assignment is silently ignored
  in some PowerShell versions:
  ```powershell
  $Err.ErrorDetails = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorDetails]::new('Your message here.')
  ```

- **Error flow patterns:**
  ```powershell
  # In process blocks (single-item cmdlets): use return
  try { ... } catch {
      $PSCmdlet.WriteError($Err)
      return
  }

  # In foreach loops (multi-item cmdlets): use continue
  foreach ($Item in $Items) {
      try { ... } catch {
          $PSCmdlet.WriteError($Err)
          continue
      }
  }
  ```

## arm-requests

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the ARM Requests rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

**All ARM calls go through `Invoke-OERArmRequest`.** The module deliberately does NOT use
`Connect-AzAccount`/`Invoke-AzRestMethod`: Az.Accounts cannot reliably reuse an externally acquired
AzAuth token. `Initialize-OERAuth -IncludeARM` caches the ARM bearer token as a SecureString and the
wrapper sends it directly, materializing the plaintext only at the request boundary and clearing it
in a `finally`. The ARM host is read from the session's cloud (`Get-OERCloudEndpoint`'s `ArmResource`
field via `-Environment`), not hardcoded to public-cloud ARM; `Invoke-OERArmRequest` keeps
`https://management.azure.com` as a documented fallback for a call made before any auth state exists,
so it fails on the missing token rather than on a null host -- do not delete that fallback. Since
Sprint 10 step 3 (BL-65, BL-96) a state without `ArmResourceUrl` takes its cloud's ARM host from
`Get-OERCloudEndpoint`, and the wrapper never sends a request without an ARM token: it refuses it
after its two gates, before the send, with the existing `ArmTokenAcquisitionFailed` -- the no-state
fallback is therefore refused too.

A 429, and a 503 carrying `Retry-After`, are retried with a bounded backoff whose constants mirror
the Graph wrapper's name for name (`ThrottleWaitBudgetSeconds` 300 per request/page,
`CallDeadlineSeconds` 900 per call, `ThrottleRetryHardCap` 10, single waits clamped to 1..120 s).
**The two transports are deliberately MIRRORED, never shared** -- their error shapes differ, and a
helper covering both would fit neither; the cost is that a wrong comment copied across is wrong
twice, so correct both files together. The bounds are enforced at the decision to wait and never by
stopping a paging loop part-way, which is also the LIMIT of what `CallDeadlineSeconds` bounds: it
caps a THROTTLED call only, and a never-throttled `-All` walk never consults it.
The ARM `Retry-After` header is read in exactly one place, `Get-ArmRetryAfterHeaderValue`, and the
header collection never leaves the wrapper. That is a convention this file states, **not** one of
the machine-checked single-owner rules above it: no gate in `tests/QA/sourcehygiene.tests.ps1`
enforces it, and none should be added that checks something weaker than the rule -- a gate green on
a second header read added elsewhere is itself a guard-shaped-but-inert test. Keep it by review.

## psscriptanalyzer

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the PSScriptAnalyzer rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

The QA gate requires **0 findings** per function file. Targeted suppressions are acceptable for
known false positives (e.g. `PSReviewUnusedParameter` on parameter-set discriminator switches)
**if and only if** a `Justification` string is provided. Never suppress a rule that hides a real
bug.

## testing-conventions

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the Testing Conventions rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

- **Tests are written in Pester 5 syntax** under `tests/Unit/{Private,Public}/`. The build resolves
  the newest Pester, and CI resolves it afresh on every run, so no version is a standing fact here;
  6.2.0 was the newest when measured on 2026-10-05. One `*.Tests.ps1` per source file. The QA gate
  (`tests/QA/module.tests.ps1`) requires a unit test file for every exported function.

- **Import by module name, not by path**, in every `BeforeAll` -- importing by path breaks the
  Sampler coverage measurement, which targets the built module. Every unit test file that imports
  the module starts with this root shape (the tripwire lines are explained below, and
  `tests/QA/testhygiene.tests.ps1` fails a file without them):

- **Mock at the module boundary:**
  ```powershell
  Mock -ModuleName Omnicit.EntraRBAC Invoke-OERGraphRequest { }
  Mock -ModuleName Omnicit.EntraRBAC Initialize-OERAuth { }
  ```

- **Reset auth state** in `BeforeEach` when testing anything that touches auth:
  ```powershell
  BeforeEach { InModuleScope Omnicit.EntraRBAC { $script:_OERAuthState = $null } }
  ```

- **Always mock `Initialize-OERAuth`** -- every public cmdlet that touches Graph or Azure calls it at
  entry, so without a mock the test attempts real authentication.

- **Mock `Invoke-OERGraphRequest`, not `Invoke-MgGraphRequest`** -- mocking the wrapper keeps the
  test at the module boundary and away from the wrapper's own retry, scrub and conversion logic. A
  `Mock -ModuleName Omnicit.EntraRBAC Invoke-MgGraphRequest` does win from the module scope, so it
  works; mock the raw SDK call only where the test is about the wrapper itself, as
  `Invoke-OERGraphRequest.Tests.ps1` is, or drives the real wrapper on purpose to observe what it
  does with a failure (the records it builds or leaves, its retries), as parts of
  `Get-OERGroup.Tests.ps1` do.

## security-hard-rules

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the SECURITY rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

6. **Never log or write access tokens.** The `Remove-OERErrorRecord -Record $PSItem` call in every
   Graph catch block is mandatory, not optional. It replaces the older `$null =
   $Error.Remove($PSItem)` idiom, which never removed anything: a module's `$Error` is a private
   list distinct from the caller's, and even against the caller's `$global:Error` the `ErrorRecord`
   bound to `$PSItem` is not the same object instance PowerShell stored there, so reference-equality
   removal silently no-ops. `Remove-OERErrorRecord` instead matches on the one part of the record
   that IS reference-stable across that boundary: its `.Exception` object.

## no-az-dependency

This section records the wording CLAUDE.md carried, before it was cut to the rules, for the Dependencies rules that link no other anchor.

What CLAUDE.md said about this rule before Sprint 11 step 11b cut it to the rule itself:

**No Az module is a dependency of this module, and no Az cmdlet is invoked at run time at all.**
ARM is called directly with an AzAuth token (`Invoke-OERArmRequest`). `Az.Resources` was declared in
the manifest until 2026-09-21 and was never used; it is gone. `Disconnect-OER` called
`Disconnect-AzAccount` behind a `Get-Command` guard until the same date, when that call was removed
too -- the module establishes no Az context, so it could only ever have reached the operator's own
session. `tests/QA/sourcehygiene.tests.ps1` now proves this from the source with an AST walk,
independently of what is installed.

`RequiredModules.psd1` still resolves `Az.Accounts`, for the TEST environment only: Pester's `Mock`
requires a command to exist, and two negative assertions depend on it -- `Connect-AzAccount`
`-Times 0` in `Initialize-OERAuth.Tests.ps1` and `Disconnect-AzAccount` `-Times 0` in
`Disconnect-OER.Tests.ps1`. That is not a runtime need, which is why it is absent from the table
above.
